ety: From Abaza абаза (abaza). See Russian абазин (abazin) for more.

s.def: A Northwest Caucasian language spoken in the Russian autonomous republic of Karachay-Cherkessia, in the Caucasus Mountains, as well as in Turkey.

ety: From Middle English, from Latin, from Ancient Greek, from Aramaic אבא/ܐܒܐ (ʼaḇā, “father”); see abbot, Abraham for more.

s.def: Father; religious superior; in the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic churches, a title given to the bishops, and by the bishops to the patriarch; a title given to Jewish scholars in the Talmudic period.
ex: The abba of the coenobion went to him and told him about the brother who had slipped up.

s.def: Alternative form of aba (Middle Eastern garment).

ety: From Arabic عَبَّاس (ʕabbās, “one who frowns a lot; untamed lion”), from عَبَسَ (ʕabasa, “to frown”), the title of the eightieth sura of the Qur'an.

s.def: A male given name from Arabic.
A surname from Arabic.
A placename affix, denoting previous ownership by an abbey
Alternative spelling of abbé.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Afroasiatic *ʔab- Proto-Semitic *ʔabw- Aramaic אַבָּא (ʾabbā)bor. Ancient Greek ἀββα (abba) Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs)bor. Latin abbās Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ih₂der. Ancient Greek -ῐᾰ (-ĭă) Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa)bor. Latin -issa Latin abbātissa Old French abeessebor. Middle English abbesse English abbess From Middle English abbesse, from Old French abeesse (French abbesse), from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbati…

s.def: A female superior or governess of a nunnery, or convent of nuns, having the same authority over the nuns which the abbots have over the monks.
ex: The abbess was always after the nuns to keep the convent immaculately clean.

s.def: A woman who runs a brothel; a woman employed by a prostitute to find clients.

ety: From French Abbeville, from Old French Abevile.

s.def: A town and commune in Somme department, Hauts-de-France, France.
A townland in Ormond Lower, County Tipperary, Ireland.
A city, the county seat of Henry County, Alabama, United States.
A city, the county seat of Wilcox County, Georgia, United States.
A city, the parish seat of Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, United States.
A town in Lafayette County, Mississippi, United States.
A city, the county seat of Abbeville County, South Carolina, United States.

ety: From A.D. 1250 in Middle English abbey, abbeye (“convent headed by an abbot”) (compare archaic English abbaye), itself borrowed from Old French abaïe, abbaïe, abeïe, abbeïe (Modern French abbaye) from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia, from Classical Latin abbās (“abbot”). Doublet of abbacy and Opatija. See abbot.

s.def: A monastery or society of people, secluded from the world and devoted to religion and celibacy, which is headed by an abbot or abbess; also, the monastic building or buildings.
ex: Near-synonym: convent
From 1199 to 1203 William Punchard was the abbot of the abbey of Rievaulx, which was part of the Cistercian order of monks.

s.def: The church of a monastery.
The office or dominion of an abbot or abbess.
A residence that was previously an abbatial building.
The abele or white poplar (Populus alba).
ex: Ab'bey. The great white poplar: one of the varieties of the Populus alba.
Abbey-lug, a branch of the abele tree.

ety: From Middle English abbot, abbod, abbed, from Old English abbat, abbad, abbod, from Latin abbās (“father”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Doublet of abba, abbé, and bwana.

s.def: The superior or head of an abbey or monastery.
ex: The newly appointed abbot decided to take a tour of the abbey with the cardinal's emissary.

s.def: The pastor or administrator of an order, including minor and major orders starting with the minor order of porter.
A layman who received the abbey's revenues, after the closing of the monasteries.
A brothel-owner's husband or lover.
A ponce; a man employed by a prostitute to find clients, and who may also act as a bodyguard or equivalent to a bouncer.

ety: From Middle English abbreviaten, from abbreviat(e) (“abbreviated”, used as the participle of abbreviaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin abbreviātus, perfect passive participle of abbreviō (“to shorten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), formed from ab- + breviō (“to shorten”), from brevis (“short”). Alternatively, a back-formation from abbreviation. Doublet of abridge.

s.def: To make shorter; to shorten (in time); to abridge; to shorten by ending sooner than planned.
To shorten by omitting parts or details.
ex: But it is one Thing, to Abbreuiate by Contracting, Another by Cutting off: […]

s.def: To speak or write in a brief manner.
To reduce a word or phrase by means of contraction or omission to a shorter recognizable form.
ex: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy is more commonly known by its abbreviated form BSE.
Alana abbreviated "involuntarily celibate" to "invcel", until someone suggested that "incel" was easier to say.

s.def: To reduce to lower terms, as a fraction.
Abbreviated.
Abbreviated, abridged, shortened.
Having one part relatively shorter than another or than the ordinary type.
An abridgment.
Shortened; made briefer.
ex: The abbreviated lesson only took fifteen minutes as opposed to an hour and a half.

s.def: Relatively short; shorter than normal, or compared to others.
Scanty, as in clothing.

ety: First attested 1400–50. From Middle English abbreviacioun, from Middle French abreviation, from Ecclesiastical Latin abbreviātiō, from Latin ad + breviō (“shorten”), from brevis (“short”). By surface analysis, abbreviate + -ion.

s.def: A shortened or contracted form of a word or phrase used to represent the whole, using omission of letters, and sometimes substitution of letters, or duplication of initial letters to signify plurality, including signs such as +, =, @.
ex: Hants is an abbreviation of Hampshire.
Americans, for example, call newcomers to Antarctica “fingies”, which comes from FNGs – a borrowed military abbreviation that means “Fucking New Guy”.

s.def: The result of shortening or reducing; abridgment.
The process of abbreviating.
A notation used in music score to denote a direction, as pp or mf.
One or more dashes through the stem of a note, dividing it respectively into quavers, semiquavers, demisemiquavers, or hemidemisemiquavers.
Any convenient short form used as a substitution for an understood or inferred whole.
ex: The phrase "civil rights" is an abbreviation for a whole complex of relationships.

s.def: Loss during evolution of the final stages of the ancestral ontogenetic pattern.
Reduction to lower terms, as a fraction.

ety: Calque of German Abderhaldensche Reaktion, named after Swiss chemist Emil Abderhalden.

s.def: The occurrence of proteolytic enzymes specific for foreign proteins introduced via parents.

Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin -dicōbf. Latin dicō Latin abdicō Latin abdicātusbor. English abdicate First…

s.def: To disclaim and expel from the family, as a father his child; to disown; to disinherit.
To reject; to cast off; to discard.
To surrender, renounce or relinquish, as sovereign power; to withdraw definitely from filling or exercising, as a high office, station, dignity; to fail to fulfill responsibility for.
ex: to abdicate the throne, the crown, the papacy
Note: The word abdicate was held to mean, in the case of James II, to abandon without a formal surrender.
The cross-bearers abdicated their service.

s.def: To relinquish or renounce a throne, or other high office or dignity; to renounce sovereignty.
ex: Though a king may abdicate for his own person, he cannot abdicate for the monarchy.

s.def: To depose.
To formally separate oneself from or to divest oneself of.

ety: First attested in 1541 as labdomen. Borrowed from Middle French abdomen as well as from its etymon Latin abdōmen, possibly from abdō (“conceal”), from ab (“away”) + -dō (“put, place”).

s.def: The belly, or that part of the body between the thorax and the pelvis, not including the back; or in some lower vertebrates, the portion between the cardiac and caudal regions.

The cavity of the belly, which is lined by the peritoneum, and contains the viscera; often restricted in humans to the part between the diaphragm and the commencement of the pelvis, the remainder being called the pelvic cavity.
ex: He was all bent over complaining of pains in the abdomen.

s.def: The fat surrounding the belly.
The posterior section of the body, behind the thorax, in insects, crustaceans, and other Arthropoda.

ety: First attested in 1746. From New Latin abdōminālis, from Latin abdōmen. Equivalent to abdomin- + -al. Compare French abdominal.

s.def: Of or pertaining to the abdomen; ventral.
ex: abdominal muscles
abdominal cavity

s.def: Characterized by or possessing a large abdomen; corpulent, pot-bellied.
Having the ventral fins under the abdomen and behind the pectoral fins.
Ventral, in describing a fin.
Belonging to the order Abdominales of fish.
The hollow portion of the torso within the abdomen, containing the abdominal organs, in mammals below the diaphragm.
Any of a group of four muscles that form the abdominal wall.
The layer of muscles that surrounds the abdominal cavity and contains the abdominal organs.

ety: From abdomino- (“abdomen”) + -plasty (“plastic surgery”).

s.def: An instance of such surgery; one operation (procedure).
The surgical removal of excess flesh from the abdomen, usually for cosmetic reasons.

ety: From abdomino- + -scopy.

s.def: Examination of the abdomen to detect abdominal disease, using an endoscope.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep Proto-Indo-European *-o Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó Proto-Italic *ap Latin abder. Latin ab- Proto-Indo-European *dewk- Proto-Indo-European *déwkti Proto-Italic *doukō Latin dūcō Latin abdūcō Latin abductusder. English abduct From Latin abductus, perfect passive participle of abduco (“to lead away”), from ab (“away”) + duco (“to lead”). * (physiology): Back-formation from abduction.

s.def: To take away by force; to carry away (a human being) wrongfully and usually with violence or deception; to kidnap.
ex: to abduct children
I was abducted by aliens.

s.def: To draw away, as a limb or other part, from the median axis of the body.

ety: From Latin abductiō(n) (“a robbing; an abduction”), from abdūcō (“to take or lead away”), from ab (“away”) + dūcō (“to lead”). By surface analysis, abduct + -ion or abduce + -tion. * (physiology): From French, from Latin abductus. * Compare French abduction.

s.def: The wrongful, and usually forcible, carrying off of a human being.
ex: the abduction of a child

s.def: A leading away; a carrying away.
The act of abducing or abducting; a drawing apart; the movement which separates a limb or other part from the axis, or middle line, of the body.
A syllogism or form of argument in which the major premise is evident, but the minor is only probable.
An alien abduction.
ex: But fear of abduction never stopped a good ufologist.

ety: From Medieval Latin abductor, from abdūcō + -tor.

s.def: A muscle which serves to draw a part out, or from the median line of the body
ex: the abductor oculi draws the eye outward.

ety: From Arabic عَبْد (ʕabd, “servant [of]”) + ال (al-, “the”).

s.def: A male given name from Arabic used by Muslims.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic عَبْدُ ٱللّٰه (ʕabdu llāh), from عَبْد (ʕabd, “servant”) + الله (allāh, “God”), literally “servant of God”.

s.def: A male given name from Arabic, feminine equivalent Amatullah; variant forms 'Abd Allah, Abd Allah, Abd' Ulah, Abd-Allah, Abdalah, Abdallah, Abdellah, Abdollah, Abdu'llah, Abdulah, Abdulla, ʻAbd Allāh.
A surname from Arabic.

ety: Etymology tree English a- Proto-Germanic *bagmaz? Proto-West Germanic *baum Old English bēam Middle English bem English beam English abeam From a- (“in the direction of”) + beam (“keel”).

s.def: On the beam; at a right angle to the centerline or keel of a vessel or aircraft; being at a bearing approximately 90° or 270° relative.
ex: We were heading S.S.W., and had a steady breeze abeam and a quiet sea.

s.def: Alongside or abreast; opposite the center of the side of the ship or aircraft.
Alongside or abreast; opposite the center of the side of the ship or aircraft.
ex: The island was directly abeam of us.
The sound shifted its place markedly, but without coming nearer. It even grew a little more distant right abeam of the lighter, and then ceased again.
The attack on the abeam ship, Louisville, killed Commander Cruiser Division Four […]

s.def: Alongside.
ex: She came abeam the crippled ship.

s.def: Beaming, shining (especially with reference to a person's face or eyes).
ex: […] the waiters fly about abeam with good will and on excellent terms with those they serve […]
When we met for another lunch […] he was all abeam with pride as he handed me a newly minted paperback reissue of Wodehouse […]

ety: From Late Latin abecedarius (from the first four letters of the Latin alphabet + -arius). Equivalent to abecedary + -an. Compare abecedary.

s.def: Someone who is learning the alphabet.
An elementary student, a novice; one in the early steps of learning.
ex: A man may alwaies continue his studie, but not schooling. O fond-foolish for an old man to be ever an Abcedarian [translating abecedaire].

s.def: Someone engaged in teaching the alphabet; an elementary teacher; one that teaches the methods and principles of learning.
A work which uses words or lines in alphabetical order.
ex: An Abecedarian is any poem constrained by alphabetical order.

s.def: Pertaining to someone learning the alphabet or basic studies; elementary; rudimentary.
Pertaining to the alphabet, or several alphabets.
Arranged in an alphabetical manner.
Relating to or resembling an abecedarius.

ety: From Middle English abedde, o bedde, from Old English on (“in”) + bedde (“bed”). Equivalent to a- (“in, on”) + bed.

s.def: In bed, or on the bed; confined to bed.
ex: Not to be abed after midnight
[She] is sick abed.
The world was awake to the 2nd of May, but Mayfair is not the world, and even the menials of Mayfair lie long abed.

s.def: On a childbed.
ex: I mean, she's brought a-bed

ety: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew הָ֑בֶל (háḇel)bor. Ancient Greek Ἅβελ (Hábel)bor. Latin Abē̆lder. Old English Ābel Middle English Abel English Abel From Middle English Abel, from Old English Ābel, from Latin Abel, from Ancient Greek Ἅβελ (Hábel), from Biblical Hebrew הֶבֶל (Héḇel, “Abel”), possibly from the homonymous word הֶבֶל (heḇel, “breath, vapor; vanity”) or from Akkadian 𒌉𒍑 (ablu, “son”).

s.def: The son of Adam and Eve who was killed by his brother Cain.
ex: And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.

s.def: A male given name from Hebrew.
A surname originating as a patronymic.
An unincorporated community in Cleburne County, Alabama, United States, named after the biblical Abel.

ety: From Middle English abelle, albell, aubel, from Old French aubel, aubiel, from Medieval Latin albellus (“white poplar”), diminutive of Latin albus (“white”). Some forms after Middle Dutch abeel, from Old French.

s.def: The white poplar (Populus alba).
ex: Six abeles i' the churchyard grow

ety: From German Aberglaube.

s.def: superstition

ety: A learned borrowing from Latin aberrātiō(n) (“relief, diversion”), first attested in 1594, from aberrō (“wander away, go astray”), from ab (“away”) + errō (“wander”). Compare French aberration. By surface analysis, aberrat(e) + -ion.

s.def: The act of wandering; deviation from truth, moral rectitude; abnormal; divergence from the straight, correct, proper, normal, or from the natural state.
ex: the aberration of youth
aberrations from theory
aberration of character

s.def: astronomy: small periodical change of position of heavenly bodies

The convergence to different foci, by a lens or mirror, of rays of light emanating from one and the same point, or the deviation of such rays from a single focus; a defect in a focusing mechanism that prevents the intended focal point.
A small periodical change of the apparent positions of the stars and other heavenly bodies, due to the combined effect of the motion of light and the motion of the observer.
A partial alienation of reason.
ex: Occasional aberrations of intellect
We see indeed the aberrations of unruly appetite

s.def: Any creature with supernatural powers not found in the organized classes of beings in a given setting.
ex: Only by submitting to the aberration could the human traders travel safely through the territory of Zularn.

s.def: A mental disorder, especially one of a minor or temporary character.
Atypical development or structure; deviation from the normal type; an aberrant organ.
A deviation of a tissue, organ or mental functions from what is considered to be within the normal range.
A defect in an image produced by an optical or electrostatic lens system.

ety: From Latin abesse (“to be absent”), infinitive of absum, from ab- (“away”) + sum (“be”, verb). Compare English absent.

s.def: The abessive case, or a word in this case.

ety: Inherited from Middle English abetter. By surface analysis, abet + -er.

s.def: Alternative form of abettor.

ety: First attested in 1528. From Anglo-Norman abeiance (“legal expectation”), from Old French abeance (“desire”) from abeër (“to gape at, aspire after”), abaer, abair (“to desire”), from a (“to”) + baër (“to gape”), bair (“yawn”), from Medieval Latin batō (“to yawn”).

s.def: Expectancy; a condition when an ownership of real property is undetermined; lapse in succession of ownership of estate, or title.
ex: The proceeds of the estate shall be held in abeyance in an escrow account until the minor reaches age twenty-one.

s.def: Suspension; temporary suppression; dormant condition.
ex: Without a plausible explanation for what might have provoked an ice age, the whole theory fell into abeyance.
The palace had previously that the duke’s military appointments were in abeyance after he stepped down from public duties in 2019.

s.def: Expectancy of a noble or armigeral title, its right in existence but its exercise suspended.
ex: The broad pennant of a commodore first class has been in abeyance since 1958, together with the rank.

ety: First attested in 1449, from Middle English abhorren, borrowed from Middle French abhorrer, from Latin abhorreō (“shrink away from in horror”), from ab- (“from”) + horreō (“stand aghast, bristle with fear”).

s.def: To regard (someone or something) as horrifying or detestable; to feel great repugnance toward.
ex: I absolutely abhor being stuck in traffic jams.
Let loue bee without dissimulation: abhorre that which is euill, cleaue to that which is good.
Many vegetarians abhor the thought of killing animals to feed themselves and also the methods by which animals are slaughtered.

s.def: To protest against; to reject solemnly.
To feel horror, disgust, or dislike (towards); to be contrary or averse (to); construed with from.
Differ entirely from.
To fill with horror or disgust.
To turn aside or avoid; to keep away from; to reject.
Strongly disliked: hated, despised.
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:abhorred.

s.def: Horrified.

ety: From abhorrent + -ence.

s.def: Extreme aversion or detestation; the feeling of utter dislike or loathing; a visceral revulsion toward something repugnant.
ex: My abhorrence of this fiend cannot be conceived.
The recognition of what pollutes evidently reflects deep-seated abhorrences, whose cause and origin are difficult to discover.

s.def: An expression of abhorrence, in particular any of the parliamentary addresses dictated towards Charles II.
A person or thing that is loathsome; a detested thing.

ety: Borrowed from Latin abhorrēns, abhorrēntis, present active participle of abhorreō (“abhor”). Equivalent to abhor + -ent.

s.def: Inconsistent with, or far removed from, something; strongly opposed.
ex: abhorrent thoughts
The persons most abhorrent from blood, and treason, and arbitrary confiscation, might remain silent spectators of this civil war between the vices.

s.def: Contrary to something; discordant.
ex: This legal, and, as it should seem, injudicious profanation, so abhorrent to out stricter principles, was received with a very faint murmur, ...

s.def: Abhorring; detesting; having or showing abhorrence; loathing.
Detestable or repugnant.
ex: If Pride, abhorrent as it is, and if Ambition, ...
That, I protest, is a doctrine psychologically impossible and ethically abhorrent.
The arts of pleasure in despotic courts I spurn, abhorrent; in a spotless heart I look for pleasure.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ud-s-? Proto-Indo-European *h₂u-s-? Proto-Germanic *uz- Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydʰeti Proto-Germanic *bīdaną Proto-Germanic *uzbīdaną Proto-West Germanic *uʀbīdan Old English ābīdan Middle English abyden English abide From Middle English abyden, from Old English ābīdan (“to abide, wait, remain, delay, remain behind; survive; wait for, await; expect”), from Proto-West Germanic *uʀbīdan, from Proto-Germanic *uzbīdaną (“to expect, t…

s.def: To have one's abode.
ex: In empty hush, in airless gloom, Mr. Knott abode, in the large room set aside for his exclusive enjoyment, and that of his attendant.

s.def: To endure without yielding; to withstand.
ex: The old oak tree abides the wind endlessly.

s.def: To bear patiently.
ex: "I never could abide shoemakers," said an old servant,—and it ended in her marrying one.
We are vegetarian leaning, dislike smoking and alcohol, cannot abide drugs.
By God sir. I will not abide another toe.

s.def: To pay for; to take the consequences of.
Used in a phrasal verb: abide by (“to accept and act in accordance with”).
ex: The new teacher was strict and the students did not want to abide by his rules.

s.def: To wait in expectation.
To stand ready for; to await someone; watch for.
ex: I will abide the coming of my lord.

s.def: To endure or undergo a hard trial or a task; to stand up under.
To pause; to delay.
To await submissively; accept without question; submit to.
To accept (a decision or law) and act in accordance with it; to conform to (a decision or law); to acquiesce to (a decision or law).
ex: I don't agree with it, but I'll abide by the decision to give the reward to her.
The defendent has abided by my ruling in good faith.

s.def: To remain faithful to (something or someone); to adhere to (an idea or plan).
ex: He may have shown his true colors, but he's supported me for years, so I'll abide by him.
She has served me loyally, abiding by my rule for almost my entire life.
To say the truth , it is often safer to abide by the consequences of the first blunder , than to endeavour to rectify it

ety: From the Ebrié expression min-chan m'bidjan (literally “I just cut the leaves”).

s.def: the largest city of Ivory Coast
The de facto capital and largest city of Ivory Coast.
The Ivory Coast government.

ety: First attested in the 1300s. From Middle English abilite (“suitability, aptitude, ability”), from Old French ableté, from Latin habilitās (“aptness, ability”), from habilis (“apt, fit, skillful, able”); equivalent to able + -ity.

s.def: A skill or competence in doing; mental power; talent; aptitude.
ex: a mixed-ability class
They are persons of ability, who will go far in life.
She has an uncanny ability to defuse conflict.

s.def: Suitableness.
Financial ability.
The quality or state of being able; capacity to do or of doing something; having the necessary power.
ex: This phone has the ability to have its software upgraded wirelessly.
This wood has the ability to fight off insects, fungus, and mold for a considerable time.

s.def: The legal wherewithal to act.
Physical power.
A unique power of the mind; a faculty.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not-”, the alpha privative) + βῐ́ος (bĭ́os, “life”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”)) + γένεσις (génesis, “origin, source; manner of birth; creation”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tis (“birth; production”)); equivalent to abio- + genesis. The words biogenesis and abiogenesis were both coined by English biologist Thomas Henry Huxley (1825–1895) in 1870 (see the quotation).

s.def: The origination of living organisms from lifeless matter; such genesis as does not involve the action of living parents.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic أَبْجَد (ʔabjad), the term for the traditional ordering of the Arabic script (from the first four letters: أ (ʔ), ب (b), ج (j), د (d)). Compare English ABC and alphabet. Linguistics sense coined by Peter T. Daniels.

s.def: A writing system for Arabic, historically also employed as a numeral system, in which there is one glyph (symbol or letter) for each consonant but vowels are not specified.
ex: In Rabghuzi's Stories of the Prophets, a teacher asked Jesus, who was seven years old at the time, to repeat the alphabet and the abjad by rote.

s.def: Any writing system in which glyphs are used to represent consonants or consonantal phonemes, but not vowels.
The system of abjad numerals; a numeral system in which the letters of the Arabic abjad are interpreted as numerals, typically used to enumerate lists and nested lists, as well as in numerology.

ety: PIE word *h₂epó The adjective is derived from Late Middle English abiect, abject (adjective) [and other forms], from Middle French abject (modern French abject, abjet (obsolete)), and from its etymon Latin abiectus (“abandoned; cast aside”), an adjective use of the perfect passive participle of abiciō (“to discard, throw away”), from ab- (prefix meaning ‘away from’) + iaciō (“to throw”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)yeh₁- (“to throw”)). The noun is derived from the adjective. Cognate…

s.def: Existing in or sunk to a low condition, position, or state; contemptible, despicable, miserable.
Of a person: cast down in hope or spirit; showing utter helplessness, hopelessness, or resignation; also, grovelling; ingratiating; servile.
Complete; downright; utter.
ex: abject failure abject nonsense abject terror

s.def: Lower than nearby areas; low-lying.
Marginalized as deviant.
ex: The disclosure of tolerance's hidden phobic lining fits in well with queer theory's embrace of the abject.

s.def: A person in the lowest and most despicable condition; an oppressed person; an outcast; also, such people as a class.
ex: [T]he subject of a tyrant's will / Became, worse fate, the abject of his own, / Which spurred him, like an outspent horse, to death.

s.def: To cast off or out (someone or something); to reject, especially as contemptible or inferior.
ex: Rather than abjecting her own fat body, the Ipecac-taking fat girl is abjecting diet culture.

s.def: To cast down (someone or something); to abase; to debase; to degrade; to lower; also, to forcibly impose obedience or servitude upon (someone); to subjugate.

ety: First attested about 1380. From Middle English accepten, borrowed from Old French accepter, or directly from Latin acceptō, acceptāre (“receive”), frequentative of accipiō, formed from ad- + capiō (“to take”). Displaced native Old English onfōn.

s.def: Lying next to, close, or contiguous; neighboring; bordering on.
ex: Because the conference room is filled, we will have our meeting in the adjacent room.
For quotations using this term, see Citations:adjacent.

s.def: Just before, after, or facing.
ex: The picture is on the adjacent page.

s.def: Related to; suggestive of; bordering on.
ex: It would be false to suggest CBD is nothing more than an obsession for reiki-adjacent bicoastal millennials.
He’s [Timothée Chalamet is] smug and entitled. He’s dismissive of opera and ballet. He’s Kardashian-adjacent.

s.def: Something that lies next to something else, especially the side of a right triangle that is neither the hypotenuse nor the opposite.
ex: Again, the key colors have twice the area of the adjacents.
Picking out the opposite, the adjacent, and the hypotenuse[…]

s.def: Next to; beside.
ex: The house adjacent to the school was demolished.
A notice was sent to the house adjacent the school.

s.def: Related to; suggestive of; bordering on.

ety: From Georgian აჭარა (ač̣ara); see there for more.

s.def: An autonomous republic of Georgia located in its southwestern corner, bordered by Turkey to the south and by the Black Sea to the west. Predominantly populated by Muslim Georgians. Capital: Batumi.

s.def: Of or relating to or functioning as an adjective.
ex: adjectival syntax
adjectival noun

s.def: Of or relating to procedure, especially to technicalities thereof.
An adjectival phrase or clause.

ety: From Middle English adjectif, adjective, from Old French adjectif, from Latin adiectivus, from adiciō + -īvus, from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + iaciō (“throw”). The Latin word adiectivus in turn was a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπιθετικόν (epithetikón, “added”), a derivative of the compound verb ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi), from which also comes epithet.

s.def: A word that modifies a noun or noun phrase or describes a noun’s referent.
ex: The words “big” and “heavy” are English adjectives.
"They'll have to invent new adjectives when I come back. You wait!"
"We have fallen into the culture of adjectives and adverbs, and we have forgotten the strength of nouns," he said.

s.def: A dependent; an accessory.
ex: it must be an adjective of dain

s.def: Adjectival; pertaining to or functioning as an adjective.
Applying to methods of enforcement and rules of procedure.
ex: The whole English law, substantive and adjective.

s.def: Needing the use of a mordant to be made fast to that which is being dyed.
Incapable of independent function.
To make an adjective of; to form or convert into an adjective.
ex: In English, instead of adjectiving our own substantives, we have borrowed, in immense numbers, adjectived signs from other languages[…]

s.def: To characterize with an adjective; to describe by using an adjective.
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:adjective.

ety: Borrowed from Russian аджи́ка (adžíka), from Abkhaz аџьыка (adžəkʼa); see there for more.

s.def: A hot, spicy but subtly flavoured paste often used to flavour food, mainly in the Caucasian regions of Abkhazia and Samegrelo.

ety: From Anglo-Norman adjoindre, from Latin adiungō.

s.def: To extend an algebraic object (e.g. a field, a ring, etc.) by adding to it an element not belonging to it and then ensuring closure, for example by also adding all finite power series of the element.
ex: The field adjunction #92;mathbb#123;Q#125;(#92;pi) can be obtained from #92;mathbb#123;Q#125; by adjoining #92;pi to #92;mathbb#123;Q#125;.

s.def: To share a common boundary or border with; to be physically contiguous to (a piece of land or property).
ex: The living room and dining room adjoin each other.
It's at this point that these three neighbourhoods adjoin.
'[…] The land was so very desirable for me in every respect, so immediately adjoining my own property, that I felt it my duty to buy it. […]'

ety: From Middle English ajournen, from Old French ajorner (French ajourner), from the phrase a jor (nomé) ("to an (appointed) day").

s.def: To postpone.
ex: The trial was adjourned for a week.

s.def: To defer; to put off temporarily or indefinitely.
ex: It is a common practice […]to adjourn the reformation of their lives to a further time.

s.def: To end or suspend an event.
ex: The court will adjourn for lunch.
The Form of this motion is, “When this assembly adjourns, it adjourns to meet at such a time.”
When it's time for the fallout / And Saint Peter calls us all out / We'll just drop our agendas and adjourn

s.def: To move as a group from one place to another.
ex: After the dinner, we will adjourn to the bar.

ety: From Middle English ajugen, adjugen, from Old French ajugier, from Latin adiudicare. Doublet of adjudicate.

s.def: To declare to be.
To deem or determine to be.
To award judicially; to assign.
To sentence; to condemn.
ex: on failure of payment of the fines adjudged against them […] for which he shall be so adjudged to imprisonment
no man ought to be adjudged to death, but by the Laws established in this your Realm

ety: Borrowed from Latin adiūdicō, adiūdicātus, from ad + iūdicō (“to judge”). Doublet of adjudge.

s.def: To decide, rule on, or settle as a judge.
ex: In North Carolina, provisional ballots are adjudicated to determine whether the voter was eligible to cast the ballot.

s.def: To act as a judge.
To seize or convey as security.

ety: Etymology tree English adjudicate Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -tor Latin -ātor Old French -eorbor. Middle English -our ▲ Latin -torlbor. English -or English adjudicator From adjudicate + -or.

s.def: One who adjudicates.

ety: From Latin adiunctus, perfect passive participle of adiungō (“join to”), from ad + iungō (“join”). Doublet of adjoint.

s.def: An appendage; something attached to something else in a subordinate capacity.
A person associated with another, usually in a subordinate position; a colleague.
Ellipsis of adjunct professor.
An unmalted grain or grain product that supplements the main mash ingredient.
A quality or property of the body or mind, whether natural or acquired, such as colour in the body or judgement in the mind.
A key or scale closely related to another as principal; a relative or attendant key.
A phrase within a clause or sentence that is grammatically dispensable but not semantically so, modifying the meaning.

A graphic element that modifies another, such as (in Linear B script) a small syllabogram that is attached to a logogram as an abbreviation of an adjective that modifies that logogram (rather than as a phonetic complement that disambiguates the logogram).
A constituent which is both the daughter and the sister of an X-bar.
Symploce.

ety: From Late Middle English adjuren (“to bind (oneself or someone) by oath to do something; to entreat or implore (someone); to question (someone) under oath”), from Anglo-Norman adjurer, Middle French adjurer, and Old French ajurer (“to bind (oneself or someone) under oath; to entreat or implore (someone)”) (modern French adjurer), and from their etymon Latin adiūrāre, the present active infinitive of adiūrō (“to take an oath”) (whence Late Latin adiūrō (“to entreat or implore (someone); to conju…

s.def: To formally command or request (someone) to do something, either in the name of a deity, or to suffer a curse or punishment if they do not comply; to bind (someone) under oath; to charge.
To earnestly advise or urge (someone); to exhort.
ex: Party members are adjured to promote awareness of this problem.

s.def: To earnestly appeal to (someone, or a deity); to entreat, to implore.
ex: The Rabbis adjured her to endow the young man with his former virility, but she vehemently refused to do so.

s.def: To summon (the Devil or an evil spirit); to invoke; also, to exorcize (the Devil or an evil spirit).
To summon the Devil or an evil spirit; also, to exorcize the Devil or an evil spirit.

ety: From Middle English ajusten, borrowed from Middle French adjuster, or Old French, from Latin ad (“to, up to, towards”) + iustus (“correct, proper, exact”); Equivalent to ad- + just. Probably influenced in sense by Old French ajouster (cf. modern ajouter), from Vulgar Latin *adiuxtāre, from Latin iuxta. The Middle English originally meant "to correct, remedy" in the late 14th century, and was reborrowed from Middle French in the early 17th century. According to another view on the etymology, the…

s.def: To modify.
ex: Morimoto's recipes are adjusted to suit the American palate.

s.def: To improve or rectify.
ex: He adjusted his initial conclusion to reflect the new data.

s.def: To settle an insurance claim.
To change to fit circumstances.
ex: Most immigrants adjust quickly to a new community.
She waited for her eyes to adjust to the darkness.

s.def: An adjustable hand tool for tightening and loosening nuts and bolts.

The assessment, by an insurance company, of a claim; the settlement of such a claim.
The action of adjusting something.
The settling or balancing of a financial account.
ex: The credit card company made an adjustment to my account to waive the late fee.

s.def: The behavioral process of balancing conflicting needs, or needs against obstacles in the environment.
ex: When Jim graduated, he found adjustment to the working world difficult.

ety: Probably in part from Spanish ayudante and in part from Portuguese ajudante (“assistant, helper, aide”), nominal uses of present participial adjectives from respectively ayudar and ajudar, from Latin adiūtō (“to help, assist”), with remodeling after its present participle adiūtāns (acc. adiūtantem). The stork's name is derived from the military sense, owing to its marchlike stiff gait when on ground.

s.def: An assistant.
A lower-ranking officer who assists a higher-ranking officer with administrative affairs.
Either the greater or the lesser adjutant, stork species of the genus Leptoptilos, family Ciconiidae, native to India and Southeast Asia.
Assistant; who helps a higher-ranking officer.
ex: adjutant officer

s.def: Alternative form of ad lib.
Alternative form of ad lib.

ety: From ad + -man.

s.def: A person in the business of devising, writing, illustrating or selling advertisements.
ex: . . . Tad Allagash, a stripling adman and Manhattan party animal with inexhaustible supplies of Bolivian Marching Powder (coy for cocaine).

ety: From Middle English administren, from Old French aminister, from Latin administrare (“to manage, execute”), from ad (“to”) + ministrare (“to attend, serve”), from minister (“servant”); see minister.

s.def: To apportion out, distribute.
ex: [Let zephyrs] administer their tepid, genial airs.
Justice was administered between man and man with an exactness and purity not before known.

s.def: To manage or supervise the conduct, performance or execution of; to govern or regulate the parameters for the conduct, performance or execution of; to work in an administrative capacity.
ex: For forms of government let fools contest: / Whate'er is best administered is best.

s.def: To minister (to).
ex: administering to the sick
A fountain […] administers to the pleasure as well as the plenty of the place.

s.def: To settle, as the estate of one who dies without a will, or whose will fails of an executor.
To give, as an oath.
ex: Swear […] to keep the oath that we administer.

s.def: To give (a drug, to a patient), be it orally or by any other means.
ex: We administered the medicine to our dog by mixing it in his food.

s.def: To cause (a patient, human or animal) to ingest (a drug), either by openly offering or through deceit.
ex: A noxious drug had been administered to him.

ety: From Middle English administracioun, from Old French administration, from Latin administratio, from administrare; see administer; compare French administration. Equivalent to administrate + -ion.

s.def: The act of administering; government of public affairs; the service rendered, or duties assumed, in conducting affairs; the conducting of any office or employment; direction.

The executive part of government; the persons collectively who are entrusted with the execution of laws and the superintendence of public affairs; the chief magistrate and his cabinet or council; or the council, or ministry, alone, as in Great Britain.
ex: Successive US administrations have had similar Middle East policies.

s.def: The country's government under the rule of a particular leader.
ex: The Obama administration
The Duterte administration

s.def: A body that administers; a body of administrators.
The act of administering, or tendering something to another; dispensation.
ex: the administration of a medicine, of an oath, of justice, or of the sacrament
oral administration of insulin

s.def: Management.
An arrangement whereby an insolvent company can continue trading under supervision.
ex: The company went into voluntary administration last week.

der: administration of the fulness of times

ety: From administrate + -ive.

s.def: Of or relating to administering or administration.
ex: administrative costs
administrative delays
administrative error

s.def: All the laws that pertain to the administrative agencies of government.

s.def: One who administers affairs; one who directs, manages, executes, or dispenses, whether in civil, judicial, political, or ecclesiastical affairs; a manager.
One who is responsible for software installation, management, information and maintenance of a computer or network.
A person who manages or settles the estate of an intestate, or of a testator when there is no competent executor; one to whom the right of administration has been committed by competent authority
ex: For quotations using this term, see Citations:administrator.

ety: From Middle English admyrable, partly from Middle French admirable and partly from its etymon, Latin admirābilis. By surface analysis, admire + -able.

s.def: Deserving of the highest esteem or admiration; estimable.
ex: It's admirable that Shelley overcame her handicap and excelled in her work.

s.def: Good or heroic.
ex: The act of putting out the burning fires was admirable.

s.def: The quality, state, or an example of being admirable.

s.def: The appointed commander of a navy, regardless of formal title.
A high rank in the British and American Navies, NATO grade OF-9, equivalent ranks in other navies, in coast guards, etc.
The commander of a naval squadron or fleet, regardless of formal rank.

The commander of a fishing or merchant fleet, particularly (historical, Canada) a captain granted special privileges in exchange for bringing the first ship of a given fishing season to certain harbors in Newfoundland.
Any of several species of nymphalid butterflies of the genera Kaniska, Limenitis and Vanessa.
The shell of the Conus ammiralis; the cone shells of various other species displaying similarly intricate banding.
Synonym of flagship: an admiral's ship in a fleet, the command or largest ship in a naval or commercial fleet.
Synonym of emir, a Muslim commander or prince.
ex: The Saracen admiral, Balán... held court in the Castillo de Aguas Muertas...

s.def: Any of several varieties of pear, the trees which produce them.
The highest rank in the Royal Navy and other Commonwealth navies, NATO grade OF-10, currently only ceremonial.
Synonym of fleet admiral.

Middle English admiral English admiral Proto-Germanic *skapjaną Proto-Germanic *-skapiz Proto-West Germanic *-skapi Old English -sċiepe Middle English -schipe English -ship English admiralship From admiral + -ship.

s.def: The state, property, or office of being an admiral.

ety: From French amirauté, for an older amiralté (“office of admiral”), from Late Latin admīrālitās. See admiral. Analyzable as admiral + -ty.

s.def: The office or jurisdiction of an admiral.
The department or officers having authority over naval affairs generally.
The court which has jurisdiction of maritime questions and offenses.
The system of jurisprudence of admiralty courts.
The building in which the lords of the admiralty, in England, transact business.

ety: From Middle English admiracion, borrowed from Middle French admiration, or directly from Latin admīrātiō, from prefix ad- (“to, towards”) + mīrō (“to look at”) + -ātiō. Compare the verb admire, and US dialectal terms miration and mirate.

s.def: A positive emotion combining wonder and approbation; the regarding of another as being wonderful; a feeling of respect for another's skills or attributes, as one might look on a hero or role model.
ex: admiration of a war hero
They looked at the landscape in admiration.
A lady’s imagination is very rapid; it jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony in a moment.

s.def: Wondering or questioning (without any particular positive or negative attitude to the subject).
ex: Lear. Your name, fair gentlewoman? Goneril. This admiration, sir, is much o’ th’ savour Of other your new pranks.
[…] Admiration seized All Heaven, what this might mean, and whither tend, Wondering;

s.def: Cause of admiration; something to excite wonder, or pleased surprise.

ety: From Middle English admyren, borrowed from Middle French admirer, from Latin admīror, from ad + mīror (“wonder at”).

s.def: To regard with wonder and delight.
To be amazed at; to view with surprise; to marvel at.
ex: The poor fellow, admiring how he came there, was served in state all day long […].
examples rather to be admired than imitated

s.def: To look upon with an elevated feeling of pleasure, as something which calls out approbation, esteem, love or reverence.
To estimate or value highly; to hold in high esteem.
ex: to admire a person of high moral worth
to admire a landscape
He'd always been (very) much admired by his colleagues.

s.def: To be enthusiastic about (doing something); to want or like (to do something). (Sometimes followed by to.)
ex: I'm not sayin' she's touched the Devil, now, but I'd admire to know what books she reads and why she hides them — she'll not answer me, y' see.
And I'd admire seeing this creek become a sort of stopping place for geese of one sort and another.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French admissible. Equivalent to admit + -ible

s.def: Capable or deserving to be admitted, accepted or allowed; allowable, permissible, acceptable.
Describing a heuristic that never overestimates the cost of reaching a goal.

ety: Borrowed from Latin admissio, admissionis; compare French admission. See admit.

s.def: The cost or fee associated with attendance or entry.
ex: There is no way he has seen that show, the admission is more than he makes in a week.

s.def: The act or practice of admitting.
Permission to enter, or the entrance itself; admittance; entrance; access
ex: I request admission for two adults.

s.def: The granting of an argument or position not fully proved; the act of acknowledging something asserted; acknowledgement; concession.

Acquiescence or concurrence in a statement made by another, and distinguishable from a confession in that an admission presupposes prior inquiry by another, but a confession may be made without such inquiry.
A fact, point, or statement admitted; as, admission made out of court are received in evidence
Declaration of the bishop that he approves of the presentee as a fit person to serve the cure of the church to which he is presented.

ety: From Middle English admitten, amitten, borrowed from Old French admettre, amettre (“to admit”), from Latin admittō (“to allow entrance, inlet”, literally “to send to”), from ad- + mittere (“to send”).

s.def: To allow to enter; to grant entrance (to), whether into a place, into the mind, or into consideration.
ex: to admit a serious thought into the mind
to admit evidence in the trial of a cause
A ticket admits one into a playhouse.

s.def: To allow (someone) to enter a profession or to enjoy a privilege; to recognize as qualified for a franchise.
ex: to admit an attorney to practice law
The prisoner was admitted to bail.

s.def: To concede as true; to acknowledge or assent to, as an allegation which it is impossible to deny (+ to).
ex: the argument or fact is admitted
He admitted his guilt.
She admitted taking drugs / she admitted to taking drugs.

s.def: To be capable of; to permit. In this sense, "of" may be used after the verb, or may be omitted.
ex: The words do not admit such a construction.
Four bells admit twenty-four changes in ringing.
There is no tree admits of transplantation so well as the Elm, for a tree of twenty years growth will admit of a remove.

s.def: To give warrant or allowance, to grant opportunity or permission.
ex: Circumstances do not admit of this.
The text does not admit of this interpretation.

s.def: To allow to enter a hospital or similar facility for treatment.

ety: Etymology tree English admitted Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder. Proto-Germanic *-līkaz Proto-Germanic *-ê Proto-Germanic *-līkê Proto-West Germanic *-līkē Old English -līċe Middle English -ly English -ly English admittedly From admitted + -ly.

s.def: As is acknowledged to be true; by general admission; confessedly.
ex: Admittedly, vandalism is a bit of a problem.
She was admittedly the one who killed the baron.
Adopting a computerlike countermeasure for a problem enabled by computer algorithms is admittedly an unnatural practice.

s.def: Signals a concession followed by a counterpoint usually headed by but.
ex: It's only a theory, admittedly, but it might work.
Admittedly he can't swim, but he still loves going to the seaside anyway.

ety: From Latin admixtūra, from admixtus, past participle of admisceō (“to mix in”), from misceō (“to mix”). Analyzable as ad- + mixture.

s.def: An instance of admixing, a mixing in of something.
ex: The admixture of vanilla extract in the dough improved the pastries' flavor.

s.def: A mixture, in some contexts
A mixture, in some contexts:
ex: Background EEG demonstrates an admixture of theta and delta waves.

ety: Inherited from Middle English a(d)monisshen (adapted through -ishen (“-ish”) from earlier amonesten), from Old French amonester (modern French admonester), from an unattested Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *admonestāre, from Latin admoneō (“to remind, warn”), from ad- + moneō (“to warn, advise”).

s.def: warn or notify of a fault; exhort
To inform or notify of a fault; to rebuke in a serious tone; to tell off.
ex: Better is a poore and a wise child, then an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished.
And further, by these, my sonne, be admonished: of making many bookes there is no end, and much studie is a wearinesse of the flesh.
[…] But then things take a turn, the men starting to keel over as Walder seems to admonish them for leaving certain threads hanging. […]

s.def: To advise against wrongdoing; to caution; to warn against danger or an offense.
To instruct or direct.

ety: From Middle English amonicioun, from Old French amonicion, from Latin admonitio, stem of admonere. The -d- was restored in English in the 17th century.

s.def: A rebuke by an authority that one has erred and should not persist in one's actions.
ex: But modesty cannot be implanted by admonition only—the elders must set the example.
Lenin repeats this admonition several times, and its purport is clear.

ety: From Latin admonitōrium (“admonition, reminder”).

s.def: Of or pertaining to an admonition; serving to reprove, warn or advise.
ex: He wagged an admonitory finger at the culprit.

ety: From Northern Middle English at do (“to do”), infinitive of do, don (“to do”), see do. Influenced by an Old Norse practice of marking the infinitive by using the preposition at, att (compare Danish at gå (“to go”)). More at at, do.

s.def: Trouble; troublesome business; fuss, commotion.

ety: Etymology tree Egyptian ḏbt Demotic Egyptian tb Coptic ⲧⲱⲃⲉ (tōbe)der. Arabic طُوبَة (ṭūba) Andalusian Arabic طُوبَة Andalusian Arabic طُوبder. Spanish adobebor. English adobe From Spanish adobe, from Arabic اَلطُّوب (aṭ-ṭūb), from Sahidic Coptic ⲧⲱⲃⲉ (tōbe, “brick”), from Demotic Egyptian ⁠⁠ (tb, “brick”), from Egyptian Db-b-t:O39 (ḏbt, “brick, block, ingot”).

s.def: An unburnt brick dried in the sun.
ex: Many people in Texas and New Mexico live in adobe houses.
“Find me a nice, clean adobe wall,” says he, “and send Senor Rompiro up against it.”
Stone sidewalks, little more than a ledge in width, ran along the base of the mean and monotonous adobe houses.

s.def: The earth from which such bricks are made.
A house made of adobe brick.
ex: The snow-dusted mesas and million-dollar adobes look enchanting as ever[…].

ety: From Middle English adolescence, from Old French adolescence, from Latin adolēscentia, from adolēscēns (“young”); see adolescent.

s.def: The transitional period of physical and psychological development between childhood and maturity, beginning at the onset of puberty and with an endpoint defined either legally (at the age of majority, such as 18 in many jurisdictions) or psychocognitively (at various ages, depending on individual e…
ex: Near-synonyms: teenagehood, teenhood, teenagerhood, teenagedom, teenagerdom, teendom
During adolescence, the body and mind go through many complex changes, some of which are difficult to deal with.

ety: First attested ?1440, from Middle English adolescent, from Middle French adolescent or directly from Latin adolescentem, accusative form of adolescens, present participle of adolēscere (“to become adult, grow up”), from ad- (“to”) + alēscere (“to grow or become nourished”). The adjective first appeared in 1785.

s.def: Of, relating to, or at the age of adolescence; at the stage between being a child and an adult.
ex: Schools, unless discipline were doubly strong, / Detain their adolescent charge too long.

s.def: A person who is in adolescence; someone who has reached puberty but is not yet an adult.
ex: It may be wartime, but Miss Adolescent wants her fun!
‘A healthy adolescent might be expected to produce five hundred billion blood cells a day.’

ety: From Middle French adopter, from Latin adoptō; ad + optō (“to choose, desire”), equivalent to ad- + opt.

s.def: to take by choice into relationship, as, child, heir, friend, citizen

ety: From Middle English affecten, from Latin affectāre, from Latin affectus, the participle stem of Latin afficere (“to act upon, influence, affect, attack with disease”), from ad- + facere (“to make, do”). By surface analysis, af- + Latin -fect.

s.def: To influence or alter.
ex: The experience affected me deeply.
The heat of the sunlight affected the speed of the chemical reaction.
The climate affected their health and spirits.

s.def: To move to emotion.
ex: He was deeply affected by the tragic ending of the play.
A consideration of the rationale of our passions seems to me very necessary for all who would affect them upon solid and pure principles.

s.def: Of an illness or condition, to infect or harm (a part of the body).
ex: Hepatitis affects the liver.

s.def: To dispose or incline.

s.def: To tend to by affinity or disposition.

s.def: To assign; to appoint.

ety: From Middle English affermen, from Old French afermer, affermer, from Latin affirmare, adfirmare (“to present as fixed, aver, affirm”), from ad (“to”) + firmare (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”). By surface analysis, af- + firm.

ety: From Old French afermacion, from Latin affirmare (“to assert”). Doublet of affirmatio.

ety: From Middle English afeld, a-felde, o felde, on felde, from Old English on felde (“afield”, literally “in (the) field”), equivalent to a- (“on”) + field.

His latest remarks went far afield of any mainstream conception.

s.def: On the field.
ex: We now have both teams afield and can begin the match.

s.def: Out in the open.
ex: The merchant was much interested in my journey, and thought it dangerous to sleep afield.
Meanwhile, witch Tituba, Tonight you sleep afield, molest not this house. Return here early for your judgement.

On fire (often metaphorically).

Often preceded by set.
ex: He who sent (If He sent) all those hearts aflame?

ex: Workmen employed in the alcohol plant rushed out, their clothing aflames^([sic – meaning aflame]) and many groping their way, blinded by the fire.

Through nights while great darkness, / I aflamed killed beasts' heads, […]
I had intended, […] to refresh my mind, wearied with long study, when a burning desire to read and learn aflamed me afresh …

s.def: Chiefly in the present participle: to be in flames or on fire; to blaze, to flare up.

concrete jungle fires / that mirror this unruly blaze / aflamed / in my heart

ety: From A(spergillus) fla(vus) + toxin.

s.def: Any of a family of mycotoxins, produced by molds of the Aspergillus genus, that can be toxic, carcinogenic, mutagenic or teratogenic; typically found as contaminants of animal food or peanuts.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Hellenic *ə- Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-)der. English a- English float English afloat From a- + float.

s.def: In or into a state of floating.
ex: You have so little Brains, that a Penn’orth of Butter melted under ’um, would set ’um afloat:
[…] I went down to my Boat, got the Water out of her, and got her afloat, loaded all my Cargo in her, and then went Home again for more;
Oh why is heaven built so far, / Oh why is earth set so remote? / I cannot reach the nearest star / That hangs afloat.

s.def: In, or while in, a vessel at sea or on another body of water; at sea.
ex: […] that trade […] may likewise employ many useful hands both ashore and afloat,
They was the roughest crew afloat, was Flint’s; the devil himself would have been feared to go to sea with them.
Navy chow ashore is rarely as good as it is afloat, and for enlisted men it is usually much worse.

s.def: Under water (bearing floating objects).
In or into circulation or currency.
ex: setting a lie aflote
[…] I shall not be judged fairly; it will get afloat that I am not a good girl,

s.def: In or into a condition of stimulation, arousal, confusion, bewilderment, etc.
ex: No angry passions rise to disturb the silent progress of the work, […] no irritable humours are set afloat:
[…] they knew how to abstain from the overdose of liquor that sets the brain afloat and loosens the tongue.

s.def: Floating.
ex: A rubber duck and other toys were afloat in the bath.
On such a full sea are we now afloat; / And we must take the current when it serves, / Or lose our ventures.

s.def: In, or found while in, a vessel at sea or on another body of water.
ex: […] that trade […] may likewise employ many useful hands both ashore and afloat,

s.def: Floating in the air; flowing freely; not tied, braided, etc. (of hair or clothing)
ex: her black hair loose and a-float down her dazzling white neck
unbound silvery-gold tresses afloat beneath a jeweled coronet
[…] she roars down the street, dreads and feathers and cape afloat,

s.def: Covered with water, bearing floating objects.
ex: The decks are afloat.

ex: I can hear / Your heart a-flutter over the snow-hills;

s.def: Filled or covered (with something that flutters).
ex: The day being warm and sultry, the balcony was all aflutter with the feather fans of the ladies of the family and their attendants,
When Sammy returned from Virginia, after an interminable gray trip back up U.S. 1, he found their house in Midwood aflutter with bunting.

s.def: In a state of tremulous excitement, anticipation or confusion.
ex: […] she rose, all a-flutter within, it is true, but with a face as nearly sedate as the inborn witchery of her eyes would allow.

ex: Possibly some chemical experiment was afoot; possibly----Well, it was no business of mine to speculate upon why he wanted it.
“Has anyone seen Laszlo? I can't find him anywhere. And it's really not like him.” “Oh... Laszlo's missing, eh?” “Yeah.” “Mm, the game is afoot.”

s.def: Walking or running; using the feet for locomotion, as opposed to on horseback or riding in a vehicle.
ex: "The dogs were no sooner let loose, than the hare was afoot."

s.def: That is on foot, in motion, in action, in progress.
ex: Sunny moves through these final days quickly, easily, buoyed by routine even though change is afoot in all directions.
“These poor exocomps are being tortured with meaningless, repetitive tasks. I knew there was foul play afoot.”

ex: The princess is next in line to the throne after the prince.

ex: […] there are only two girls. No after claps, like my sister Gresham’s little ‘Teddy;’ […]

s.def: A sweet food, drink, or tobacco product consumed at the end of a meal.
ex: Never speak of dinner as “grub,” “hash” or “trough-time,” nor refer to the dessert as “an after-clap.”

s.def: An additional adverse event that occurs unexpectedly after an earlier one was thought to be over and done with.
ex: What plaguy mischiefs and mishaps Do dog him still with after-claps!
AFTERCLAPS, unpleasant things coming after affairs which were supposed ended.
Strange to say, the gale, after easing to a mild breeze, recrudesced in a sort of afterclap.

ex: To spare a little for an after clappe Were not improuidence.

s.def: The consequence (often, but not always, adverse) of an action or event.

A sound that follows another, especially a loud noise, such as thunder.
ex: […] the storm wore gradually away, now and then only a faint after-clap grumbled in the distance […]
Music brought up our rear: the chanting of the old doctor, the clap and echoing after-clap of his rhythm sticks as he shuffled out of his sorry camp.

s.def: A change or attempted change to an agreement after it has been entered into; an additional charge (especially one over and above the previously agreed-upon price).

s.def: A conscious existence after death; a supernatural life that follows one's natural life, in some worldviews.

s.def: The place believed to be inhabited by people who have died.
ex: You'll reunite later, somewhere in the afterlife.

ety: From a- + gape. First known use by John Milton in Paradise Lost (1667).

s.def: Any sound or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a warning sound to arouse attention; a warning of danger.
ex: Sound an alarm in my holy mountain.

s.def: A device intended to warn or give notice of approaching danger.
ex: The fire alarm is located high on the wall to prevent tampering.

s.def: A sudden attack; a disturbance.
ex: Lord Marshal, command our officers-at-arms Be ready to direct these home alarms.

s.def: Sudden surprise with fear or terror caused by the apprehension of danger; a feeling of heightened alertness to risk.
ex: His actions caused alarm among all the other people in the store, who hurried to leave.
Alarm and resentment spread through the camp.

s.def: A mechanical device for awaking people or rousing their attention.
ex: The clock radio is a friendlier version of the cold alarm by the bedside.

s.def: An instance of an alarm ringing, beeping or clanging, to give a noise signal at a certain time.
ex: Last night's alarm turned out to be nothing, but it was terrifying at the time.

s.def: To keep in excitement; to disturb.
To call to arms for defense.
To give (someone) notice of approaching danger or necessary action; to rouse to vigilance; to put on the alert.
ex: The sudden drop in temperature should alarm you into taking precautions.
Her illness started to alarm the doctors, who ordered more tests.

s.def: A clock designed to sound an alert at a preset time, primarily to wake someone from sleep.
ex: "I should suggest an alarum clock," he said briskly. "I always use one myself for fear of oversleeping.[…]"

ety: From Middle English alarom, from Old Italian all'arme (“to arms, to the weapons”), from Latin arma, armorum (“weapons”).

s.def: A danger signal or warning.
ex: Just another forum, then, sounding the usual alarums on the looming threat from global warming?

s.def: A call to arms.
An alarm clock.
ex: Ten minutes passed by the measure of the battered old alarum on the dresser shelf before the young man returned.

s.def: To sound alarums, to sound an alarm.

ety: From Middle English alas, from Old French a las (French hélas), from a (“ah”) + las, from Latin lassus (“weary”). Compare Dutch helaas, North Frisian ielas, West Frisian eilaas.

s.def: Used to express sorrow, regret, compassion, grief, resignation, or disappointment.

ety: From Russian Аля́ска (Aljáska, “Alaska”), in turn from Aleut alaxsxaq (“a mainland”, literally “that toward which the action of the sea is directed”), composed of alag (“pertaining to the sea”) + -sxa (nominalizing suffix, yields 'the objective of action expressed by the root') + -q (nominalizing suffix). Commonly misattributed to Russian ала (ala) + -ский (-skij, adjectival suffix).

s.def: US state

ety: From Romanian Alba Iulia.

ety: From the Middle English expression al be it (that), itself shortened from althagh it be that (“although it be that”), and thus composed from al (“completely, entirely”, literally “all”) + be (3rd person singular present subjunctive of been (“to be”)) + it.

ety: From Persian البرز (alborz); see that entry for more. Doublet of Elbrus.

ex: Though most interviews are aired in ten-minute segments, very often they are longer than that specific time allotment.

s.def: The allowance of a specific amount of money or other credit of a particular thing to a particular person.
ex: Maynard used to help before he got sick, but there was no income except what I brought in my allotment.

ety: Back-formation from allotropy, as allo- + -trope, from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”), and τρόπος (trópos, “way, manner”).

s.def: Any form of an element that has a distinctly different molecular structure to another form of the same element, with different physical properties and often different chemical properties.
An other form, a different shape of a lexical unit.
An alternative shape of a cognitive structure.

ety: From allo- + -tropic, compare French allotropique.

s.def: Describing a form of an element that exhibits allotropy.
ex: Graphite and diamond are allotropic forms of carbon.

ex: to allow a servant his liberty; to allow a free passage; to allow one day for rest

s.def: To present something as possible or reasonable.
ex: The event allows of only one interpretation.

s.def: To permit, to give permission to.
ex: I will allow my son to be absent.

s.def: To not bar or obstruct.
ex: Although I don't consent to their holding such meetings, I will allow them for the time being.
Smoking (is) allowed only in designated areas.

ex: to allow a right; to allow a claim; to allow an appeal

"Well, that rug does match the wallpaper," he allowed.

ex: to allow a sum for leakage
How much will you allow on my old jalopy?

s.def: To make an allowance, to take into account when making plans.
ex: When calculating a budget for a construction project, always allow for contingencies.

s.def: To render physically possible.
ex: The inlet allowed a facility to bring the money in a boat secretly and at night to the very foot of the hill.

s.def: To praise; to approve of; hence, to sanction.
ex: Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers
We commend his pains, condemn his pride, allow his life, approve his learning.

s.def: To sanction; to invest; to entrust.

ex: you sent a large commission to Gregory de Cassado, to conclude, without the King's will or the state's allowance

s.def: Acknowledgment.
ex: The censure of the which one must in your allowance overweigh a whole theater of others.

s.def: An amount, portion, or share that is allotted or granted; a sum granted as a reimbursement, a bounty, or as appropriate for any purpose.
ex: her meagre allowance of food or drink
Being a volunteer is unpaid, but we get accommodation and a living allowance of 100 euros a week.

s.def: Abatement; deduction; the taking into account of mitigating circumstances.
ex: to make allowance for his naivety
After making the largest allowance for fraud.

s.def: A deduction from the gross weight of goods, such as to discount their container's weight or per a custom differing by country.
ex: Minus the allowance, the total came to thirteen tons.

s.def: A permitted reduction in the weight that a racehorse must carry.
ex: On the Flat, an apprentice jockey starts with an allowance of 7 lb.

s.def: A permissible deviation in the fineness and weight of coins, owing to the difficulty in securing exact conformity to the standard prescribed by law.
Approval; approbation.
ex: […]gave allowance where he needed none

s.def: License; indulgence.
ex: this Allowance for their Transgressions

s.def: A sum of money allotted to a wife for her separate maintenance, especially alimony granted upon a legal separation or divorce.
ex: '[…] Her legal allowance was not adequate to her fortune, nor sufficient for her comfortable maintenance […].

ety: Borrowed from Middle French alloy, aloy, from Old French aloi, from aloiier, from Latin alligō.

s.def: A metal that is a combination of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal, a base metal.
A metal of lesser value, mixed with a metal of greater value.
ex: gold without alloy

s.def: An admixture; something added which stains, taints etc.
ex: Metrodorus said that in sadnesse there is some aloy of pleasure.
The sole grievance and alloy thus removed in the prospect of Harriet’s welfare, she was really in danger of becoming too happy for security.
The fatal word was never heard, and their happiness seemed without alloy.

s.def: A fusion, marriage or combination.

ety: From all + spice, as it was thought to combine the flavors of various other spices.

s.def: A spice; the dried and ground unripe fruit of Pimenta dioica, thought to combine the flavours of several spices, such as cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves.
Pimenta dioica, an evergreen tree of tropical America with aromatic berries.

ety: From Middle French alluder, from Latin alludere (“to play with or allude”), from ad + ludere (“to play”). See also al-.

s.def: To refer to something indirectly or by suggestion; to invoke it by implication rather than mention.
ex: First, she alluded to her husband as "the man at home looking after the children". Then she referred to him as "my George".

ety: From Middle English aluren, from Old French aleurer, alurer, from a (“to, towards”) (Latin ad) + leurre (“lure”). By surface analysis, al- + lure.

s.def: The power to attract, entice; the quality causing attraction.
To entice; to attract.
ex: A tender voice his wondring ear allur'd.

s.def: Gait; bearing.
ex: Harper's Magazine The swing, the gait, the pose, the allure of these men.

s.def: The walkway along the top of a castle wall, sometimes entirely covered and normally behind a parapet; the wall walk.

ety: By surface analysis, allure + -ing.

s.def: present participle and gerund of allure

s.def: An indirect reference; a hint; a reference to something supposed to be known, but not explicitly mentioned.

ety: From Latin alluvius (“alluvial”), from alluviō (“an overflowing, inundation”), from alluō (“wash against”). By surface analysis, alluvium + -ial.

s.def: Pertaining to the soil deposited by a stream.
A deposition of sediment over a long period of time by a river; an alluvial layer.
Alluvial soil; specifically, in Australia, gold-bearing alluvial soil.

ety: Borrowed from Latin alluviō.

s.def: The increase in the area of land due to the deposition of sediment (alluvium) by a river.

ety: From Medieval Latin alluvium (“matter deposited by flowing water”), neuter of alluvius (“deposited by a river”), from Latin alluviō (“washing upon, overflowing”). See also al-.

s.def: soil, clay, silt or gravel deposited by flowing water, as it slows, in a river bed, delta, estuary or flood plain

ety: From Middle English allien, alien (“to form an alliance, associate, join; to become an ally; to introduce (someone) as an ally; to marry; to become related (to someone); to attack, engage in combat; to combine; (cooking) to combine ingredients, especially to bind them together”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman alier, allier, Middle French alier, allier [and other forms], and Old French alier (“to join together, unite; to alloy (metals); (cooking) to combine ingredients”) (modern French all…

s.def: A person, group, state, etc., which is associated or united by treaty with another for a common (especially military or political) purpose; a confederate.
ex: The two countries were allies in World War I.

s.def: To unite or form a connection between (people or things), as between families by marriage, or between states by confederacy, league, or treaty.
ex: She died; and her place was supplied by a German princess nearly allied to the Imperial House.

s.def: Chiefly followed by to or with: to connect or form a relation to (someone or something) by similarity in features or nature.
To join or unite (oneself or itself) against, with, etc., someone or something else.
Chiefly followed by with: to enter into an alliance or unite for a common aim.
ex: Whatever injuries […] the Athenians have done me I forgive. […] If they will ally with me, rebuild the temples I have burnt.

s.def: A person who co-operates with or helps another; an associate; a friend.
ex: He became the ally of a boy named Aubrey Mills and founded with him a gang of adventurers in the avenue.

s.def: Something regarded as connected with or related to another thing by similarity in features or nature.
ex: the pretty Pansy then Ile tye / Like Stones some Chaine inchasing, / And next to them their neere Alye, / The purple Violet placing.

s.def: A person, group, concept, etc., which is associated with another as a helper; an auxiliary; a supporter.
ex: [S]cience, instead of being the enemy of religion, becomes its ally.

s.def: A kinsman or kinswoman; a relative.
One's relatives; kin, kindred, relations; also, relationship through descent or marriage; kinship.

ety: From Latin alma māter (literally “nourishing mother”). Derives from the full name ("Alma Mater Studiorum Università di Bologna") of the oldest European university, the University of Bologna, founded in 1088.

s.def: A school, college, or university which a person has graduated from or attended.
ex: I’m in the place where I grew up, where my alma mater is.

s.def: A school’s anthem or song.
Any book resembling the Almagest.

ety: From Middle English almenak, from Old French almanach, from Medieval Latin almanachus, from Andalusian Arabic الْمَنَاخ (al-manāḵ, “almanac, calendar”), from Arabic الْمُنَاخ (al-munāḵ, “climate”).

s.def: A book or table listing nautical, astronomical, astrological or other events for the year; sometimes, but not essentially, containing historical and statistical information.
A handbook, typically published annually, containing information on a particular subject.
A GPS signal consisting of coarse orbit and status information for each satellite in a satellite constellation.

ety: Transliteration from Kazakh Алматы (Almatı), which is an adjective form of алма (alma, “apple”).

s.def: The largest city in and former (until 1998) capital of Kazakhstan, formerly known as Alma-Ata.
ex: Unlike Uzbekistan, which unsuccessfully pursued the 2000 summer Games, the Almaty bid was crafted by wily veterans of the process.

s.def: A region of Kazakhstan. Capital: Qonayev.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Spanish Almería, from Arabic المرية (al-Mariyya), from مَرَايَا (marāyā, “mirrors”) in reference to the settlement's initial role in the 9th century as a watchtower for Bajjana, now Pechina.

s.def: A province of Andalusia, Spain, around the city.
A city and municipality, the capital of the province of Almería, Andalusia, Spain.
A city in Tatarstan, Russia.

The tree that produces almonds.
Other plants that produce almond-like nuts:
The colour of the kernel of an almond without its shell and thin seed coat, a creamy off-white colour.
The colour of an almond still covered by its skin, a shade of brown.
Flavour or other characteristics of almond.
ex: I can't eat it if it has too much almond in it.

s.def: Anything shaped like an almond; specifically, (anatomy, archaic) a tonsil.

s.def: Brownish, resembling the colour of an almond nut.

ety: Inherited from Middle English almonde mylk.

A type of confection made from ground almonds and sugar in equal quantities, bound with some syrup or other similar substance in order to form a paste.

ety: From Middle English aumener, aulmener, from Old French almosnier, from almosne (“alms”), from Latin eleemosyna. See alms, Almosen.

Alms are distributed from the weekly collection.
c. 1779, Alban Butler, Lives of the Saints St. Antoninus never refused an alms which was asked in the name of God.

ety: From Middle English almeshous, almassehous, equivalent to alms + house.

s.def: A building of residence for the poor, sick or elderly of a parish. Originally founded by the Church, and usually funded by charitable donations.

ety: From the genus name taxonomic name Alocasia.

s.def: Any of several tropical Asian plants, of the genus Alocasia, having heart- or arrowhead-shaped leaves.

ety: From Old English alwe (“fragrant resin of an East Indian tree”), from Latin aloē, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓λόη (ălóē), from Hebrew אָהָל (ʾāhāl) or related Aramaic forms, ultimately from Tamil அகில் (akil); reinforced in Middle English by Old French aloes.

Any plant of the large and variable genus Aloe.
Misnomer for any large, vaguely aloe-like plant, such as Agave.
ex: In mercy I put a bullet through his skull, and he fell sprawling among the aloes.

s.def: A strong, bitter drink made from the juice of such plants, used as a purgative.

ety: From Old Norse á lopti (“in the sky”); equivalent to a- + loft.

ex: high winds aloft

s.def: Above, overhead, in a high place; up.
ex: Someone's turned the chest out alow and aloft.
He noticed that he still held the knife aloft and brought his arm down, replacing the blade in the sheath.

s.def: In the top, at the masthead, or on the higher yards or rigging.
ex: I think you said something concerning the manner in which yonder ship has anchored, and of the condition they keep things alow and aloft?

ety: From Ancient Greek ἀλογία (alogía, “absurdity; confusion; irrationality; speechlessness”). By surface analysis, a- + -logia.

s.def: A general lack of additional, unprompted content in normal speech, a common symptom of schizophrenia.

s.def: Good wishes, love, compassion, peacefulness and affection.
ex: When I got back to Hawaii, a feeling of aloha flooded me, and my anxiety vanished.
Uncle Onio exemplifies aloha by sharing his broad knowledge of Hawaiian culture and weaving techniques.

s.def: An utterance of aloha (see Interjection, below).
Expressing good wishes when greeting or parting from someone; hello; goodbye.

s.def: By oneself, solitary.
ex: I can't ask for help because I am alone.
It is not good that the man should be alone.
Alone on a wide, wide sea.

s.def: Lacking peers who share one's beliefs, experiences, practices, etc.
ex: Senator Craddock wants to abolish the estate tax, and she's not alone.
I always organize my Halloween candy before eating it. Am I alone in this?
If you’ve been feeling overwhelmed by it all, you’re not alone.

s.def: Apart from, or exclusive of, others.
ex: God, […] by whose alone power and conversation we all live, and move, and have our being.

s.def: Mere; consisting of nothing further.
Unique; rare; matchless.
ex: Pardon me, Proteus, all I can is nothing / To her, whose worth makes other worthies nothing; / She is alone.

s.def: Without outside help.
ex: The job was too hard for me to do alone.

s.def: By oneself; apart from, or exclusive of, others; solo.
ex: She walked home alone.

s.def: Focus adverb, typically modifying a noun and occurring immediately after it.
ex: The president alone has the power to initiate a nuclear launch.
They must be told, that the ultimate authority, wherever the derivative may be found, resides in the People alone;
The Senate (A.U.C. 514) decreed that the eldest son alone should bear his father's praenomen.

ex: The kine[…]went along the highway.
In the lightness of my heart I sang catches of songs as my horse gayly bore me along the well-remembered road.
Swiftly and silently he made his way along the track which ran through the meadows.

ex: John played the piano and everyone sang along.

ex: Don't stop here. Just move along.
