ety: From Middle English loof (“weather gage, windward direction”), probably from Middle Dutch (Compare Dutch loef (“the weather side of a ship”)), originally a nautical order to keep the ship's head to the wind, thus to stay clear of a lee-shore or some other quarter, hence the figurative sense of "at a distance, apart".

s.def: At or from a distance, but within view, or at a small distance; apart; away.
ex: Sisyphus also I saw, with unwelcomest taskage tormented, / Toilsomely hoisting aloof, unassisted, a ponderous round stone.
The noise approaches, tho' our palace stood Aloof from streets, encompass'd with a wood

s.def: Without sympathy; unfavorably.
Either physically or emotionally remote: distant, standoffish.
Away from; clear of.
ex: Rivetus […] would fain work himself aloof these rocks and quicksands.

ety: Borrowed from Latin alōpecia, from the Ancient Greek ἀλωπεκία (alōpekía, “fox-mange”), from ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx, “fox”) + -ία (-ía, a formative ending used in Ancient Greek, especially used in naming diseases).

s.def: A loss of hair (especially on the head) or loss of wool or feathers, whether natural or caused by disease.
ex: “Jada, can’t wait for GI Jane 2,” Rock said in an apparent reference to her shaved hair, which is a result of the hair loss condition alopecia.

s.def: Baldness.
A deficiency of the hair, which may be caused by a failure to grow or loss after growth.

ety: From Middle English aloud, a loude (“aloud”), equivalent to a- + loud or a- + loude (“sound”).

s.def: With a loud voice, or great noise; loudly; audibly.
ex: Try speaking aloud rather than whispering.

s.def: Audibly, as opposed to silently/quietly.
ex: speaking aloud rather than thinking thoughts privately
He read the letter aloud. Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.

s.def: Spoken out loud.
ex: When you are meditating with sound, it can be aloud or it can be silent

ety: Late Middle English, back-formation from alps pl, via French from Latin Alpes (“high mountains, especially those of Switzerland”). Compare Old Saxon elbon (“Alps”), Old High German Alpūn (“Alps”); Old High German alba (“alp, mountain”)).

s.def: A very high mountain. Specifically, one of the Alps, the highest chain of mountains in Europe.
ex: There is a great alp of sand, one hundred metres high, between the pines and the ocean, […]

s.def: An alpine meadow.
ex: At the alp of Khyarkuti, a wide flat at the junction of several glens[…]

ety: Borrowed from Spanish alpaca, from Aymara allpaqa.

s.def: A sheep-like domesticated animal of the Andes, Vicugna pacos, in the camel family, closely related to the llama, guanaco, and vicuña.
Wool from the alpaca, with strong very long fibres and coloring from black to brown to white.
ex: A lady in frayed alpaca, carrying a house-flannel, came to hearken.

s.def: A garment made of such wool.

ety: Borrowed from German Alpenstock, from Alpen (“alps”) + Stock (“stick”), early 19th c.

s.def: A stout adjustable walking stick with a metal point, used by mountain climbers and walkers in hilly or uneven terrain.

Latin alpha: the Latin letter Ɑ (minuscule: ɑ).
The name of the symbols Α and α used in science and mathematics, often interchangeable with the symbols when used as a prefix.
ex: I will attempt to make an alpha particle ("α-particle") with the Large Hadron Collider.

s.def: The return of a given asset or portfolio adjusted for systematic risk.
A person, especially a male, who is dominant, successful and attractive; (see alpha male).

An angle of attack.

s.def: The brightest star in the southern constellation of Centaurus. It is actually a binary star with Proxima Centauri as a third component.

An early preview version of a program or application, typically unstable, but useful to show what the product will do. Sometimes no more features are added after this release, but bug fixes continue. This release comes after a pre-alpha version and before a beta version.

ety: Borrowed from taxonomic name Alyssum, from Ancient Greek ἄλυσσον (álusson).

ety: From Portuguese ama (“female nurse”), from Medieval Latin amma (“wet nurse, amma”), perhaps an alteration of Latin mamma, of imitative origin, or from Ancient Greek.

ety: From a- (prefix with the sense ‘at; in; on; with’, used to show a state, condition, or manner) + main (“force, power, strength”). Main is derived from Middle English mayn (“strength”), from Old English mæġen (“strength”), from Proto-Germanic *maginą (“might, power, strength”), *maginaz (“strong”), from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“to be able”).

s.def: With all of one's might; mightily; forcefully, violently.
ex: The palfrey was as fleet as wind, And they rode furiously behind. They spurr'd amain, their steeds were white; And once we cross'd the shade of night.

s.def: At full speed; also, in great haste.
ex: The heavy rain it hurries amain And heaven and the hurricane.

s.def: Out of control.
Exceedingly; overmuch.

ety: From Latin āmanuēnsis (“secretary”), from ab- (“from, off (of)”) + manus (“hand”) + -ensis (“of or from (a place)”), early 17th c.

ety: Coined by Milton, originally meaning "unfading", as amaranth + -ine, from Ancient Greek ἀμάραντος (amárantos, “unfading”). Later used for color. First attested in the 1660s.

ety: From Middle English *amassen (found only as Middle English massen (“to amass”)), from Anglo-Norman amasser, from Medieval Latin amassāre, from ad + massa (“lump, mass”). See mass.

to gather a great quantity of; to accumulate.

ety: From amass + -er.

ety: Borrowed from French amateur, from Latin amātor (“lover”), from amāre (“to love”).

ety: From French embuscade, from Italian imboscata from the past participle of imboscare (“to ambush”), from Vulgar Latin *imbosco (“I hide, ambush”) (see there for more), from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, heavy stick”). Compare ambush. More at bush.

ety: From modified Latin amnesia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”), a noun derivation from μιμνήσκω (mimnḗskō, “to remind, to remember”) prefixed with the alpha privative.

s.def: Forgetfulness; cessation of remembrance of wrong; oblivion.
To grant a pardon (to a group).

An asexual.

ety: From Latin amomum.

s.def: Historical records; chronicles; history.
ex: the short and simple annals of the poor
It was one of the most critical periods in our annals.

s.def: A periodic publication, containing records of discoveries, transactions of societies, etc.
ex: Annals of Science

ety: From Middle English anelen, onelen, from Old English onǣlan (“to burn, ignite, set fire to, consume, heat, enlighten, incite, inflame, inspire, kindle”), from Proto-Germanic *ana (“on”) + Proto-Germanic *ailijaną (“to burn”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“to burn”). The double-N spelling may have arisen by analogy with Latinate verbs like announce, annex, and annul. The word is related to Old English onāl (“that which is burnt, burning; incense”), Old English āl (“fire, burning”), Iceland…

s.def: To subject to great heat and then (often slow) cooling, and sometimes reheating and further cooling, for the purpose of rendering less brittle; to temper; to toughen.
ex: A properly made, fully sintered and fully annealed metal clay piece should be able to stand up to any traditional metalsmithing technique.

s.def: To cool glass slowly, to minimize internal stress.
To burn colors onto a glass or other surface.
To make a double-stranded nucleic acid by pairing a single strand with a complementary strand.
To strengthen or harden.
ex: The experience annealed them, strengthening their resolve.

s.def: An act of annealing.
Alternative form of anele (“anoint”).
ex: MABEL: Is he to die, unshriven – unannealed?

ety: From French annélidé, coined by French naturalist Lamarck.

s.def: Any of various wormlike animals, of the phylum Annelida, having a segmented body; they include the earthworm and the leech.
ex: Incarcerated in earth-filled boxes, the hapless annelids face execution in the morning. Death by immersion in fishponds, death by cruel hooks.
The polychaetous annelid species complex of Neanthes acuminata has a widespread distribution, with names depending on geographic location.

s.def: of, or relating to these creatures

ety: Borrowed from French annexe, from Latin annexus. More at Etymology 2. See also an-.

s.def: An addition, an extension.
An appendix to a book or document.
An addition or extension to a building.
An addition to the territory of a country or state, from a neighboring country or state, normally by military force.
To add something to another thing, especially territory; to incorporate.
ex: The ancient city of Petra was annexed by Rome.
In 1910, he returned to Korea, which had by this time been annexed by Japan.

s.def: To attach or connect, as a consequence, condition, etc.
ex: to annex a penalty to a prohibition, or punishment to guilt
Annexed to my feeling of guilt was a sense of having let my familiy down.
Under Edward the Second, the Commons began to annex petitions to the bills by which they granted subsidies

s.def: To join; to be united.
To take something without permission (informal)
ex: I returned to resume my place but my assistant had already annexed my chair.

ety: From Medieval Latin annexation-, stem of annexatio (“action of annexing”), from past participle of annecto.

s.def: Addition or incorporation of something, or territories that have been annexed.
A legal merging of a territory into another body.

ety: Borrowed from Latin annihilātus, perfect passive participle of annihilō (“to reduce to nothing”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad (“to”) + nihil (“nothing”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also an-.

s.def: To reduce to nothing, to destroy, to eradicate.
ex: An atom bomb can annihilate a whole city.

s.def: To react with antimatter, producing gamma radiation and (for higher-mass reactants, especially composite particles such as protons) lighter particles (such as pions, muons, and neutrinos).
To treat as worthless, to vilify.
To render null and void; to abrogate.
To cause to become zero by means of an annihilator operator.

ety: From Middle English anniversary, from Medieval Latin anniversāria (diēs), anniversārium, from anniversārius (“yearly”), from annus (“year”) + versus, past participle of vertere (“to turn”).

s.def: A day that is an exact number of years (to the day) since a given significant event occurred. Often preceded by an ordinal number indicating the number of years.
ex: Today is the fiftieth anniversary of the end of the war.
A 'millennium' is a thousand-year anniversary.
As we mark the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, we must seize this moment to build a genuine culture of free expression for all.

s.def: day an exact number of years since an event
A day subsequent in time to a given event by some significant period other than a year (especially as prefixed by the amount of time in question).
ex: The occasion was the six-month anniversary of the Aug. 8 coup that brought General Óscar Humberto Mejía Victores to power.
Jonathon proposed to his [Jess's] mom on their three-month anniversary of meeting and married her on their fourth.

ety: From the Latin annō Hegirae (“in the year of the Hijra”), from annō (“in the year”) (the ablative of annus (“year”)) + Hegirae (“of the Hijra”) (genitive of Hegira (“the Hijra”)). Formed in imitation of the Christian Anno Domini.

s.def: In the year of the Hijra (counted by the Islamic calendar).
ex: This valuable manuscript was copied Anno Hegirae 1100 (a.d. 1688).

ety: From Latin annotātus, past participle of annotāre (an alternative form of adnotāre), from ad- (“to”) + notāre (“to mark, note”). By surface analysis, an- + note + -ate.

s.def: To add annotation to.
ex: He read the poem carefully, then annotated it with a felt pen.

ety: From Latin annotātiōnem, accusative singular of annotātiō (“remark, annotation”), from annotātus, perfect passive participle of annotō (“note down, remark”). Equivalent to annotate + -ion.

s.def: A critical or explanatory commentary or analysis.
ex: She added an annotation in the margin to clarify the text.

s.def: A comment added to a text.
ex: make an annotation
The manuscript was filled with helpful annotations.
The teacher asked students to submit essays with proper annotation.

s.def: The process of writing such comment or commentary.
Metadata added to a document or program.
Information relating to the genetic structure of sequences of bases.

s.def: To give public notice of, especially for the first time; to make known.
ex: Her [Queen Elizabeth’s] arrival was announced through the country by a peal of cannon from the ramparts.

s.def: To pronounce; to declare by judicial sentence.
ex: Publish laws, announce / Or life or death.

s.def: To act as announcer for (an event, usually sports).
ex: Our coach has retired, but occasionally he still announces the games.

s.def: To act or work as an announcer.
ex: Our coach has retired, but occasionally he still announces.

ety: From Middle French annoncement. By surface analysis, announce + -ment.

s.def: An act of announcing, or giving notice.
ex: He raised his hand to make his announcement and said, "Excuse me everyone, I have an announcement to make."

s.def: That which conveys what is announced.
ex: This announcement was made during the first training session.

s.def: The content which is announced.
ex: The announcement implied that somebody needed a spare Toshiba charger.

s.def: One who makes announcements.
ex: radio announcer

s.def: To molest; to harm; to injure.
ex: to annoy an army by impeding its march, or by a cannonade
tapers put into lanterns or sconces of several-coloured, oiled paper, that the wind might not annoy them
Say, what can more our tortured souls annoy / Than to behold, admire, and lose our joy?

s.def: A feeling of discomfort or vexation caused by what one dislikes.
ex: [I]f she says he was defeated, why he had better, a great deal, have been defeated, than give her a moment's annoy.

s.def: That which causes such a feeling.
ex: The home far and away, the distance where lives joy, / The cure, at once and ever, of world and world's annoy; […]

ex: Having flies in your bedroom when you're trying to sleep is really annoying.

ety: First attested around 1382, borrowed from Late Latin annuālem, annuālis, related to Latin annālis, adjective form of annus (“year”). Used to categorize plants since 1710.

s.def: Happening once every year.
ex: an annual general meeting; an annual publication

s.def: Of, for, or relating to a whole year, often as a recurring cycle; determined or reckoned by the year; accumulating in the course of a year; performed, executed, or completed over the course of a year. See also circannual.
ex: an annual salary; average annual profits; the annual course of the sun

s.def: Having a life cycle that is completed in only one growing season, e.g., beans, corn, marigold. See Annual plant in Wikipedia. Compare biennial, perennial.
Living or lasting just one season or year, as certain insects or insect colonies.

An annual publication; a book, periodical, journal, report, comic book, yearbook, etc., which is published serially once a year, which may or may not be in addition to regular weekly or monthly publication.
ex: I read the magazine, but I usually don't purchase the annuals.

s.def: An annual plant; a plant with a life span of just one growing season; a plant which naturally germinates, flowers and dies in one year. Compare biennial, perennial.
ex: I can't wait to plant my annuals in the spring.

s.def: A medical checkup taking place once a year.
ex: Some routine annuals take a half hour and cost about $30.

s.def: A pantomime taking place once a year.
ex: From 1852 until 1888 he was the author of every Drury Lane pantomime, or "Annuals" as in his old fashioned way he preferred to […]

s.def: Amount of time expressed as the number of days per year that an employee is entitled to be away from work.
ex: If you're already thinking ahead to next year's holidays you can double your break and get a whopping 52 days off using just 26 days of annual leave.

s.def: The use of such days to be away from work; on holiday or vacation.
ex: The European Working Time Directive, brought into UK law in 1998, says workers should receive their 'normal' pay when they go on annual leave.

ety: annuity + -ant

s.def: The recipient of an annuity.

ety: From French annuité, from Medieval Latin annuitās, from Latin annuus (“annual”). Cf. annuality.

s.def: A right to receive amounts of money regularly over a certain fixed period, in perpetuity, or, especially, over the remaining life or lives of one or more beneficiaries.

ety: From Middle English annullen, from Old French anuller, from Latin annullō (“annihilate, annul”), from ad (“to”) + nūllus (“none, not any”).

s.def: To formally revoke the validity of.
To dissolve (a marital union) on the grounds that it is not valid.
To cancel out.
ex: They tried to reassure me but I was not able to annul my fears.

ety: From Latin ānulāris (“ring-shaped”); (possibly through French annulaire), from ānulus (“ring”).

s.def: Pertaining to, or having the form of, a ring: in the shape of an annulus.
ex: Near-synonyms: oval; round; toroid
annular fiber
If anybody snickers, put 'em in their place by reminding them that the annular wing is a very old aeronautical principle.

s.def: Banded or marked with circles.
a solar eclipse in which the thin outer disk of the sun can be seen as a ring around the moon

ety: Borrowed from New Latin annulatus, from Latin ānulātus.

s.def: Having an annular form or shape.
Describes a fern sporangium that has an annulus.
Describes a mushroom with an annulus on the stipe.
One of the Annulata.
To cause (something) to undergo an annulation reaction (a reaction which forms a ring of atoms).

s.def: The formation of a ring

ety: From Latin ānnulus (“small ring”) + -et.

s.def: A small ring.
A ring-shaped molding at the top of a column.
A small circle borne as a charge in coats of arms.
Charissa obscurata (also Scotch annulet), a moth of the family Geometridae.

ety: Recorded since the 15th century (sense destruction); from Middle English anullement, partly from annullen (from Middle French annuller, from Latin annūllāre, from ad (“to”) + nūllus (“not any, nothing”) + verbal ending -āre) + -ment (“means to”) (from Latin -mentum) and partly from Middle French annullement. By surface analysis, annul + -ment.

s.def: An act or instance of annulling.
ex: marriage annulment
grant an annulment
petition for annulment

s.def: The state of having been annulled.
An invalidation of something, especially a legal contract.
A legal (notably judicial) declaration that a marriage is invalid; the procedure leading to it.
Total destruction.

ety: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ānnulus, a misspelling of Latin ānulus (“ring, especially one worn on a finger”), from ānus (“ring”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂-n-o- (“ring”), from an uncertain root) + -ulus (diminutive suffix). The plural form annuli is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ānnulī.

s.def: A ring- or donut-shaped area, object, or structure.

A ring of fibrous tissue; specifically (cardiology), such a ring around an opening of a heart valve, to which the valve leaflets and muscle fibres of the atria and ventricles are attached; an annulus fibrosus cordis.

A ring of light in a celestial body, especially when caused by an annular eclipse (for example, when the Sun and Moon are in line with the Earth, but the Moon does not completely cover the Sun's disc).

A structure surrounding a sporangium (or part of it) which shrinks and causes it to rupture for spore dispersal; specifically, in a fern: a structure around about two-thirds of the sporangium consisting of differentially thick-walled cells which dry and distort the sporangium; and in a moss: a comp…
The membranous remnants of a partial veil which leaves a ring on the stem of a mushroom.

A dark ring on a fish's scale that is formed when a fish's growth rate slows down in the winter due to low food intake and the scale's circuli move closer to one another. The dark ring is used to estimate the fish's age, approximately one year per annulus.
The region in a plane between two concentric circles of different radii.
Any topological space homeomorphic to the region in a plane between two concentric circles of different radii.
In a well such as an oil well or water well: the space between a pipe or tube and any pipe, tube, casing, or sides of a hole surrounding it.

ety: From annunciātus, Medieval Latin alternative spelling of annuntiātus, past participle of Latin annūntiāre. Doublet of announce.

s.def: To announce.

ety: From Middle English annunciacion, annunciation, from Latin annuntiātiō and Old French anonciacion.

s.def: The act of annunciating.
ex: "Not in the least; I saw it was an abbreviation from the first annunciation of the marriage, as communicated by the earl of Rotheles; here it is."

ety: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) and ὁδός (hodós, “path”), forming the New Greek compound ἄνοδος (ánodos). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, an- (“up, forward, away”) + -ode (“way”).

s.def: the electrode of an electrochemical cell at which oxidation occurs

It can have either a positive or a negative voltage with respect to cathode of the same polarized device (depending on whether the devic…
(by extension) The electrode at which chemical oxidation of anions takes place, usually resulting in the erosion of metal from the electrode.
The electrode which collects electrons emitted by the cathode in a vacuum tube or gas-filled tube.
That electrode of a semiconductor device which is connected to the p-type material of a p-n junction.

ety: From Middle English anodine, from Medieval Latin anōdynos (“stilling or relieving pain”), from Ancient Greek ἀνώδυνος (anṓdunos, “free from pain”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain”). Adjective sense “noncontentious” probably through French anodin (“harmless, trivial”), of same origin.

s.def: Capable of soothing or eliminating pain.
ex: The citrate is the most efficient as an alkali, but irritates some stomachs, the liquor the most anodyne, the acetate the most diuretic.

s.def: Noncontentious, blandly agreeable, unlikely to cause offence or debate.
ex: Near-synonyms: harmless, neutral
It all became so routine, so anodyne, so dull.
States typically like to stick to anodyne messages, like saving wildflowers or animals. But every so often a controversy crops up.

s.def: Soothing or relaxing.
ex: Classical music is rather anodyne.

s.def: Any medicine or other agent that relieves pain.
A source of relaxation or comfort.
ex: The air was heavy with the perfume of the flowers, and their beauty seemed to bring him an anodyne for his pain.

ety: From Middle English enointen, anointen, borrowed from Old French enoint, past participle of enoindre (“to anoint”). Doublet of inunct.

s.def: To smear or rub over with oil or an unctuous substance; also, to spread over, as oil.
ex: He anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay.

s.def: To apply oil to or to pour oil upon, etc., as a sacred rite, especially for consecration.
ex: Anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.

s.def: To choose or nominate somebody for a leading or otherwise important position, especially formally or officially, or as an intended successor.
To mark somebody as an official ruler, especially a king or queen, as a part of a religious ceremony.

ety: From Late Latin anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμᾰλος (anṓmălos).

s.def: Deviating from the normal; marked by incongruity or contradiction; aberrant or abnormal.
ex: statistically anomalous
highly anomalous
The scientist noted an anomalous result in the data.

s.def: Of uncertain or unknown categorization; strange.
Having anomalies.

s.def: Any event or measurement that is out of the ordinary regardless of whether it is exceptional or not.

s.def: Any of various angular distances.
A defect or malformation.
A failure of a classical symmetry due to quantum corrections.
An irregularity or disproportion.

ety: From French anomie, from Ancient Greek ἀνομία (anomía, “lawlessness”), from ἄνομος (ánomos, “lawless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Popularized by French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858–1917).

s.def: Alienation or social instability caused by erosion of standards and values.

ety: From Middle English anoon, anon, anan (literally “in one (moment)”), from on (“in”) + ān (“one”). See on and one.

s.def: Straight away; at once.
ex: But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;
The dead man answered thus: “What good gift shall God give us?”, The boards answered him anon: “Flesh to feed hell's worm upon.”

s.def: Soon; in a little while.
ex: […]for as much as the same consisteth not in the extreames, but in a verie mediocritie of wealth and riches, as it shall better appeare anone.

s.def: At another time; then; again.
An anonymous person, traditionally especially a published author but now especially an internet rando.
ex: Indeed they did all they could to avoid it, coyly hiding their identities behind initials, asterisks, and anons
Every body shared in the emotion of Anons [sic] song .... Anon is sometimes man, sometimes woman....
Indeed, virtually every known playwright (and probably most of those 'anons') occupied some position in one or more of the patronage networks

s.def: A work with an unknown author.
A work without a title.
Clipping of anonymous.

ety: Coined or borrowed around 1812, from French anonyme, from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “without name”).

s.def: An anonymous person.
An assumed or false name.
A mere name; a name resting upon no diagnosis or other recognized basis.

ety: From Latin anonymus or its etymon Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “anonymous”) + -ity. Compare French anonymité.

s.def: The quality or state of being anonymous (nameless or unidentified).
ex: She's garbed her philanthropic activities in anonymity.
Now there are twenty-nine skaters on Wollman Rink Circling in singles and in pairs In this vigorous anonymity

s.def: That which is anonymous.
ex: In one sense the protagonist is the poet himself, but in another sense he is an anonymity.

s.def: The quality or state of being generally unknown, unrecognized, or uncelebrated.

Without any name acknowledged of a person responsible.
ex: an anonymous pamphlet
an anonymous subscription
anonymous author or painter

s.def: Of unknown name; whose name is withheld
ex: an anonymous author
an anonymous benefactor
No customer personal data will be retained unless it is rendered anonymous.

s.def: Lacking individuality.
ex: an anonymous office block in a soulless industrial estate

s.def: A class without a name, available only in the scope where it is defined.

Ellipsis of anorexia nervosa.

ex: intimacy anorexia; emotional anorexia

ety: From the scientific term anorexia nervosa (1957), from the symptom anorexia (“loss of appetite”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ν- (ăn-, “without”) + ὄρεξις (órexis, “appetite, desire”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-ia”), and Latin nervōsa (“nervous”).

s.def: An eating disorder characterized by self-starvation due to an irrational fear of gaining weight.

ety: From New Latin anosmia, equivalent to an- + -osmi.

s.def: Inability to smell; the inability to perceive odors.

ex: "I'll be ninety my next birthday, but Louella doesn't tell her age. Anyway, we're going to have you and Cynthia up for supper."

s.def: Used at the end of a question for emphasis, or to direct the conversation to something of more broad importance (compare with more to the point).
In any way.

s.def: In or at any location.
ex: I don't know where I left my keys. They could be anywhere.
I'd rather be anywhere else.
For many 'home' is an affectation when used anywhere that 'house' would be appropriate, as in 'Home for Sale'.

s.def: To (in the direction of) any location.
ex: Anywhere you go in France, there will be bread and wine with dinner.
I'm staying home today. I'm not going anywhere.
Are you going anywhere special this weekend?

s.def: Any location or an unknown location.
ex: Anywhere is better than here!

s.def: A person without strong cultural or social ties that are exclusive to a specific place.

s.def: In any case.
A soldier from the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (1914-1918).
The site of the landing by Anzac troops on the Gallipoli peninsula, Turkey, in WWI; Anzac Cove.
ex: After a voyage which lasted a couple of days, we arrived at the island of Imbros, some ten miles from Anzac.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἀόριστος (aóristos, “unbounded”).

s.def: A verb paradigm found in certain languages, usually an unmarked form or one that expresses the perfective or aorist aspect.
A particular verb in the aorist.
Of or pertaining to a verb in the aorist aspect.
ex: the aorist stem of a verb

s.def: A temporal feature of the verb which denotes the speaker's standpoint of the event described by the verb, as from outside of the event and seeing it as a completed whole.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ, “the arteries springing from the heart”), from ἀορτέω (aortéō), lengthened form of ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, raise”).

s.def: The great artery which carries the blood from the heart to all parts of the body except the lungs; the main trunk of the arterial system.
The liveliest part of something.

ety: From Middle English apās (“step by step, slowly; quickly, rapidly; at once, promptly”), from Old French à pas (“at a quick pace”).

s.def: Quickly, rapidly, with speed.
ex: Construction of the new offices is proceeding apace.
Ow faire Hippolita, our nuptiall houre / Drawes on apace: foure happy daies bring in / Another Moon[…]
Twilight was coming on apace and a star or two was already out, but the remains of the sunset could still be seen in the west.

s.def: Alternative letter-case form of Apache, a Parisian gangster.

ety: From Middle English apart, aparte, a-part, a part, from Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem (“to the side”).

s.def: Placed separately (in regard to space or time).
ex: We had a large bus and I had two of them at the front and two at the back, and I had to sit in the middle and keep them apart.
Others apart sat on a hill retired.

s.def: Separately, exclusively, not together.
ex: Consider the two propositions apart.

s.def: In or into two or more parts.
ex: We took the computer apart and put it back together.
Love, love will tear us apart, again.

s.def: To the side; aside.
ex: Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
Let Pleasure go, put Care apart.

s.def: Excluded from consideration.
ex: Joking apart, what do you think?

s.def: Exceptional, distinct.
ex: In aristocracies, servants are a class apart.

s.def: Having been taken apart; disassembled, in pieces.
Separate, on the side.

ety: Etymology tree Middle French a partbor. Dutch apart Proto-Indo-European *keyt-der. Proto-Germanic *haiduzder. Proto-West Germanic *-haidu Old Dutch -heit Middle Dutch -heit Dutch -heid Dutch apartheid Afrikaans apartheidbor. English apartheid Borrowed from Afrikaans apartheid (literally “separateness, apartness”) (1929 in a South African socio-political context), from Afrikaans apart (“separate”) + suffix -heid, cognate of English -hood.

s.def: The policy of racial segregation in South Africa from 1948 to 1994.
ex: She don't care about the rest at all / She's got a system they call apartheid / It keeps a brother in a subjection
The reality, however, is a disquieting and entirely white town, littered with old apartheid flags and monuments to the architects of segregation.

s.def: Any similar policy of racial segregation or separation and discrimination, particularly when in favor of a minority rule.
ex: The 1973 Apartheid Convention conferred universal jurisdiction to the state signatories to prosecute those who commit apartheid.
Jim Crow miscegenation laws enforced apartheid in marriage.

s.def: A policy or situation of segregation based on some specified attribute.
ex: In these annual reports, the religious apartheid practices in India are not mentioned at all.

s.def: To impose a policy of segregation of groups of people, especially one based on race.
ex: Yes, apartheiding the apartheiders, is what the rest of the world is doing.
Whatever the reason the blacks have for "apartheiding" Boston, whites should be all for it.
The most deadly of all ghosts are wandering over Britain and medicine, apartheiding people into superiors and nonentities.

ety: Blend of apartment + hotel.

s.def: A form of hotel having self-catering apartments instead of bedrooms or suites.

ety: From French appartement, from Italian appartamento, from Spanish apartamiento (“separation, seclusion”), equivalent to apart + -ment. See apart and -ment.

s.def: A complete domicile occupying only part of a building, especially one for rent; a flat.
ex: apartment dwellers
I am Jonathan. I am in apartment B4. — I am in apartment C2.

s.def: A suite of rooms within a domicile, designated for a specific person or persons and including a bedroom.
A room within a house.
A division of an enclosure that is separate from others; a compartment.
A conceptual space used for separation in the threading architecture. Objects in one apartment cannot directly access those in another, but must use a proxy.
A residential building containing multiple apartments or flats.

ety: From apathy + -etic.

s.def: Void of feeling; not susceptible of deep emotion.
Of, or pertaining to apatheism.
An apathetic or indifferent person, especially one who shows no interest in a particular issue.

ety: From French apathie, from Latin apathīa, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia, “impassibility”, “insensibility”, “freedom from emotion”), from ἀπαθής (apathḗs, “not suffering or having suffered”, “without experience of”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + πάθος (páthos, “anything that befalls one”, “incident”, “emotion”, “passion”). Doublet of apatheia, which was borrowed directly from Ancient Greek.

s.def: Lack of emotion or motivation; lack of interest or enthusiasm towards something; disinterest (in something).

ety: From international scientific vocabulary, from German Apatit (“apatite”). Apatit was coined by the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner (1749–1817), as follows: Ancient Greek ᾰ̓πᾰ́τη (ăpắtē, “deceit, fraud”) (as it is often mistaken for other minerals) + German -it (suffix forming nouns denoting minerals or rocks; cognate with English -ite); the German word was first used in a 1786 book. Regarding minerals that were named for being deceptive and thus confused with others, compare also fool's…

s.def: A calcium fluoride phosphate of variable composition, sometimes used in the manufacture of fertilizer, as a gemstone, and (in powdered form) as a pigment, and also produced biologically in bones and teeth.

ety: From Middle English ape, from Old English apa (“ape, monkey”), from Proto-West Germanic *apō, from Proto-Germanic *apô (“monkey, ape”), possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep- (“water”), compare Proto-Celtic *abū (“river”) (hence English place name Avon, Irish abha, Welsh afon), if the word originally referred to a "water sprite". Traditionally assumed to be an ancient loanword instead, ultimately probably from an unidentified non-Indo-European language of regions in Africa or Asia whe…

s.def: A Hominoidea primate other than a human.
An anthropoid of the superfamily Hominoidea, generally larger than monkeys and distinguished from them by having no tail.
An unintelligent or unsophisticated person, especially one who behaves irrationally or in an uncivilised manner.
ex: But he was worried about Leiter in the hands of those clumsy black apes.

s.def: One who apes; a foolish imitator.
A person who invests in meme stock, especially one who uses subreddits such as /r/wallstreetbets.
ex: I could not think of a better representation of the good in this world, let alone this r***^([sic]) band of apes on Reddit.
With the economy humming and the stock market near record highs, the “apes” are back—and “in full-on risk mode.”

s.def: To behave like an ape.
To imitate or mimic, particularly to imitate poorly.
ex: But there’s this difference; one is gold put to the use of paving-stones, and the other is tin polished to ape a service of silver.
It is not conceived as a mere “aping” in externals nor as an enacting in the sense of assuming a foreign role.
Every year a paper or a book appears, bemoaning the fate of economics and complaining about its attempts to ape physics.

s.def: Wild; crazy.
ex: We were ape over the new look.
He went ape when he heard the bad news.

ety: From French à pic (“at its summit; vertically”), compare with Italian a picco.

s.def: In a vertical line, the cable having been sufficiently hove in to bring the ship over it.
ex: Thus the good we should cherish, the bad never seek, / For death will too soon bring each anchor apeak.

ety: From ape + man.

s.def: A prehistoric man resembling an ape, especially one held to be a precursor to modern humans; a non-human australopithecine.
A reputed or legendary, large, bipedal, ape-like creature, as Bigfoot or the Yeti, or a primitive australopithecine still extant today.
A human raised from childhood by apes (generally in reference to, or in imitation of, the fictional character Tarzan).
ex: How may we judge him, by what standards, this ape-man with the heart and head and body of an English gentleman, and the training of a wild beast?
Human Nature has as its hero a caged ape man, and, like him, it has been hanging around for quite a while awaiting release.
Apes leap to and fro, ape men swing from trees, and even a giant, menacing spider gets in on the act.

ety: From Latin Ā̆pennīnus.

s.def: A mountain range in Italy, stretching 1,200 km from the north to the south of the country, along its east coast, traversing the entire Apennine Peninsula, and often called the "spine of Italy".
Alternative spelling of aperçu.

ety: Attested since the early 17th century, from Latin aperiens, present participle of aperire (“to open”).

s.def: Having a gentle laxative effect.
Serving to open or reveal.
A laxative, either in the form of a medicine or a food such as asparagus or hops, which has the effect of moving the bowels, or aiding digestion and preventing constipation.
Alternative form of apéritif.

ety: Borrowed from French apéritif. Doublet of aperitive.

s.def: An alcoholic drink served before a meal as an appetiser.

ety: From late Middle English, from Latin apertūra (“an opening”), from aperiō (“to uncover, make or lay bare”) + -tūra (“-ure”, action noun suffix). Doublet of overture and apertura.

s.def: A small or narrow opening, gap, slit, or hole.
ex: an aperture in a wall
The door was opened — ‘on the chain.’ The old lady peered at us through an aperture of about six inches.

s.def: A hole which restricts the diameter of the lightpath through one plane in an optical system.
ex: This telescope has a 100 cm aperture.

s.def: The (typically) large-diameter antenna used for receiving and transmitting radio frequency energy containing the data used in communication satellites, especially in the geostationary belt. For a comsat, this is typically a large reflective dish antenna; sometimes called an array.
The maximum angle between the two generatrices.
ex: If the generatrix makes an angle θ to the axis, then the aperture is 2θ.

ety: From ape + -ery.

s.def: The practice of aping (copying)
apish behavior.
A place where apes are kept.
ex: If you have a hippopotamus major in your brain, you are no ape, though you had four hands, no feet, and were more apish than the apes of all aperies.

ety: From New Latin āpetalus. By surface analysis, a- + petal + -ous.

s.def: Having no petals.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep-der. Proto-Italic *apeks Latin apexbor. English apex Borrowed from Latin apex (“point, tip, summit”).

s.def: The moment of greatest success, expansion, etc.
ex: the apex of civilization
It would be an intense disgust. The absolute apex of teen angst.

s.def: highest or greatest part
The highest or the greatest part of something, especially forming a point.
ex: the apex of the building

s.def: An obstacle for a horse to jump over, consisting of a triangular corner fence.
The top of the food chain.
A conical priest cap.

s.def: A condition where one does not possess a functioning "mind's eye" and cannot visualize imagery.

ety: From French aphasie, from Ancient Greek ἀφασία (aphasía), from ἄφατος (áphatos, “speechless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + φάσις (phásis, “speech”). Equivalent to a- + -phasia.

s.def: A partial or total loss of language skills due to brain damage. Usually, damage to the left perisylvian region, including Broca's area and Wernicke's area, causes aphasia.
ex: The Doctor came over in three minutes, and heard the story. ‘It's aphasia,’ he said.

ety: From New Latin aphēlium (whence English aphelium, now displaced) + -ion (used in the names of other apsides). Aphelium was formed from Ancient Greek ἀπο- (apo-, prefix meaning ‘away, from, off’) + ἥλῐος (hḗlĭos, “the sun”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“the sun”)), modelled after New Latin apogaeum (“apogee”). The plural form aphelia is from aphelion + -a (plural form of the suffix -on).

s.def: The point in the elliptical orbit of a comet, planet, or other astronomical object, where it is farthest from the Sun.
ex: [I]t follows from the theory of gravity, that the aphelia of Mercury, Venus, the Earth, and Mars, slightly progress.

ety: From New Latin aphis (plural aphides), coined by Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus in 1758. s.def: A concise or pithy, and memorable, expression of a general truth; a maxim, a saying.
A concise expression of a principle in an area of knowledge; an axiom, a precept.
The essence or heart of something.
To speak or write one or more aphorisms (noun sense 2).
ex: He was thoughtful: "Preferences define superiority," he aphorismed. "As long as preferences are not made godly edicts.[…]"
"I don't know what more to do," she confessed. "I've aphorismed my heart out and relationships have not improved one whit, it seems."

ety: From Ancient Greek ἀφορῐστικος (aphorĭstikos), equivalent to aphorist + -ic.

s.def: Of, relating to, or containing aphorisms, epigrams, or maxims; gnomic.
ex: Over and above all this, the method of the book is aphoristic; and, as might be expected from that method, without a plan; […]

ety: From a- (prefix meaning ‘not; without; opposite of’) + photic.

s.def: Having no light, especially no sunlight.
Describing that part of deep lakes and oceans where less than one per cent of sunlight penetrates and where photosynthesis is not possible.
That part of the deep body of an ocean or lake that receives insufficient sunlight for photosynthesis to be possible.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀφροδισιακός (aphrodisiakós, “venereal”), from Ἀφροδίσιος (Aphrodísios, “pertaining to Aphrodite”).

s.def: Arousing or intensifying sexual desire.
ex: Cognac, with the addition of a little paprika and the yolk of an egg, is considered an effective aphrodisiac aid.

s.def: Something, generally a food or drug, having such an effect.
ex: Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀφροδίτη (Aphrodítē) (see it for more).

s.def: A female given name from Ancient Greek.
ex: Aphrodite Jones is an American author and TV producer.

s.def: The goddess of beauty and love, born when Cronus castrated his father, Uranus, and threw his genitalia into the sea.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἄφθα (áphtha, “mouth ulcer”).

s.def: Candidiasis, oral thrush, thrush (fungal infection of the mucous membranes of the mouth caused by any species of yeast from the genus Candida).
An oral ulcer, disregarding the cause.
Foot-and-mouth disease.

ety: 19th century, from New Latin aphyllus, from Ancient Greek ἄφυλλος (áphullos, “leafless”) (ἀ- (a-) + φύλλον (phúllon)).

s.def: Having no leaves; leafless.

ety: 19th century, from Latin apiānus, from apis (“bee”).

s.def: Relating to bees.
A bee.
ex: The largest of all the apians is the humble-bee, or humming-bee (Bombus).
Whether in the world of apians or Homo sapiens, this highly concentrated super-food is indeed fit for a queen.

ety: 17th century, from Latin apiārium, from apis (“bee”).

ety: Etymology tree English api- Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *kʷélh₁eti Proto-Italic *kʷelō Latin colō Proto-Indo-European *-tew-? Proto-Indo-European *-r-eh₂? Latin -tūra Latin cultūrader. Middle French cultureder. English culture English apiculture From api- (“bee”) + culture.

s.def: The keeping and maintenance of bees for commercial reasons.

ety: Univerbation of a + piece (noun), from Late Middle English a pece. Pece is derived from Anglo-Norman pece, peece, peice, Middle French piece, and Old French pece, pice, piece (“part of a whole”) (modern French pièce); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Late Latin *pettia, *pettium (compare pecia, pecium, petia, petium (“broken piece, fragment; piece of land”)), or from their possible etymon Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis (“piece, portion; quota”).

s.def: Following a noun or noun phrase: by, for, or to each one; each by itself.
ex: Near-synonyms: all, individually, singly; piecemeal, piecewise
These melons cost a dollar apiece.
[…] Kings at a moderate reckoning Reign but 18 or 20 years a-piece one vvith another: […]

s.def: For an undetermined distance.
ex: down the road apiece

Free from, or corrected for, spherical aberration and chromatic aberration
A condition marked by the incomplete development, or entire absence, of an organ or tissue.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French aplomb (“plumb line”).

s.def: Self-confidence; poise; composure.
ex: His nonchalance and aplomb during hard times have always been his best character trait.
We can handle functions of a few variables with some aplomb and view sets of quantities totalling IO6 or IO7 with sangfroid.
Korda, preternaturally calm about everything, confronts his past with outward aplomb, but there’s an uneasiness growing in him.

s.def: The apparent elegance and precision exhibited by a confident, accomplished dancer.
The perpendicular; perpendicularity.

ety: From a- + -pnoea.

s.def: Alternative form of apnea.

Near-synonym: Ragnarok

ex: The early development of Perl 6 was punctuated by a series of apocalypses by Larry Wall.

s.def: A huge disaster; a cataclysmic event; destruction or ruin of large scope and scale.
ex: Near-synonyms: cataclysm, catastrophe, holocaust; armageddon, doomsday, end times, eschaton, judgement day, judgment day
A nuclear apocalypse would have been possible if tensions went out of control during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
Man has forgotten the soul and thus doomed his civilization to apocalypse.

s.def: The Book of Revelation.
To reveal.
To dwell on a huge disaster one expects to take place.
To bring about (a huge disaster).

ety: Borrowed from Latin apocalypticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποκαλυπτικός (apokaluptikós, “revelatory”), from ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis, “revelation”), from ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalúptō, “to reveal, uncover”).

s.def: Of or relating to an apocalypse:
ex: These bookends house a wealth of apocalyptic stories. The Bible, like some street preacher with a sign, shouts, "The end is near!"

s.def: Catachresis for apoplectic.
ex: He was apocalyptically furious.

s.def: Portending a future apocalypse (disaster, devastation, or doom).

ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin apocopē, derived from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ), ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

s.def: The loss or omission of a sound or syllable from the end of a word.
The loss or omission of the last vowel in a word, together with any consonants that follow it.

ety: From Middle English apocrypha, apocrifa, apocrif, from Late Latin apocryphus (“secret, not approved for public reading”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos, “hidden, obscure”, thus “(books) of unknown authorship”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”). Properly plural (the singular would be apocryphon), but commonly treated as a collective singular. “Apocryphal” meaning “of doubtful authenticity” is first attested in English in 1590.

Something, as a writing, that is of doubtful authorship or authority (formerly also used attributively).

ety: From the Latin apodīcticus (“proving clearly”, “demonstrative”), from the Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτικός (apodeiktikós, “affording proof”, “demonstrative”), from ἀποδείκνυμι (apodeíknumi, “to demonstrate”). ex: No religion has ever yet owed its prevalence to ‘apodictic certainty’.

ex: In "I will be coming if this weather holds up", "I will be coming" is the apodosis and "this weather holds up" is the protasis.

ety: From Middle English apperen, aperen, borrowed from Old French aparoir (French apparoir), from Latin appāreō (“to appear”), from ad (“to”) + pāreō (“to come forth, to become visible”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

ex: And God[…]said, Let[…]the dry land appear.

s.def: To come before the public.
ex: A great writer appeared at that time.

ex: We must all appear before the judgment seat.

s.def: To become visible to the apprehension of the mind; to be known as a subject of observation or comprehension, or as a thing proved; to be obvious or manifest.

ex: He appeared quite happy with the result.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French apparence, from Latin apparentia, from appareo. Morphologically appear + -ance. Doublet of apparence and apparency. Displaced native Old English hīew (“the way something looks or seems”) and ætīewednes (“act of appearing or coming into view”).

s.def: The state of being appointed to a service or office; an office to which one is appointed.
ex: the appointment of treasurer

s.def: A stipulation; an agreement; the act of fixing by mutual agreement.
A decree; a direction; an established order or constitution.
ex: to submit to the divine appointments
According to the appointment of the priests.

s.def: The exercise of the power of designating (under a power of appointment) a person to enjoy an estate or other specific property; also, the instrument by which the designation is made.
The assignment of a person by an official to perform a duty, such as a presidential appointment of a judge to a court.
Equipment, furniture.
ex: […] the house had been inhabited for years by his father, and in many of its appointments was old-fashioned and grim […]

s.def: An honorary part or exercise, as an oration, etc., at a public exhibition of a college.
ex: to have an appointment

ety: From Middle French apportionner, from Old French aporcioner, from Late Latin apportionare, from Latin ad + portio. By surface analysis, ap- + portion.

s.def: To divide and distribute portions of a whole.
ex: The controlling party had apportioned the voting districts such that their party would be favored in the next election.

s.def: Specifically, to do so in a fair and equitable manner; to allocate proportionally.
ex: The children were required to dump all of their Halloween candy on the table so that their parents could apportion it among them.

ety: Etymology tree English apportion Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English apportionment From apportion + -ment.

s.def: The act of apportioning or the state of being apportioned.
ex: The names of the prayers are given above the tunes, but there is no indication of apportionment of the text to the phrases and notes of the melody.

s.def: The allocation of direct taxation according to the population of the various states.
The distribution of members of the House of Representatives according to the population of the various states.

ety: From appose + -able.

s.def: Capable of being apposed, or applied one to another, as the thumb to the fingers of the hand; able to be brought into direct spatial opposition.

ety: Variant form of oppose.

s.def: To interrogate; to question.
ex: I shal assaye hir my-self · and sothelich appose / What man of þis worlde · þat hire were leueste.

s.def: To place next or to or near to; to juxtapose.

ex: The nymph herself did then appose, / For food and beverage, to him all best meat.

ety: From Latin appositus, past participle of adponere, from ad- + ponere (“to put, place”). See apposition.

s.def: Strikingly appropriate or relevant; well suited to the circumstance or in relation to something.
ex: Rough-neck is a capital word; it is more apposite and savory than the English navvy, and it is over-whelmingly more American.

s.def: Related, homologous.
That which is apposite; something suitable.
ex: Hugh gave the boy apples or other small apposites[…], but the child was too interested in the bishop to notice the gifts.

ety: From Middle English apposicioun, from Middle French apposition, from Latin appositiō, past participle of appōnere (“to put near”).

s.def: A construction in which one noun or noun phrase is placed with another as an explanatory equivalent, both of them having the same syntactic function in the sentence.
ex: The apposition in the title has been read as indicating that ‘Hobson-Jobson’ is equivalent to ‘colloquial Anglo-Indian words and phrases’.

s.def: The relationship between such nouns or noun phrases.
The quality of being side by side, apposed instead of opposed, next to each other.
A placing of two things side by side, or the fitting together of two things.

Appositio, the addition of an element not syntactically required.

of or being in apposition
a word or phrase that is in apposition

ety: Etymology tree English appraise Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English appraisal From appraise + -al.

s.def: The act or process of developing an opinion of value.

ety: From Middle English apreisen, from Old French aprisier (“apraise, set a price on”) (compare modern French apprécier), from Late Latin appretiare, from ad- + Latin pretium (“price, value”) (English precious), from which also appreciate, a doublet.

s.def: To determine the value or worth of (something), particularly as a person appointed for this purpose.

s.def: To consider comprehensively.

ex: At the end of the contract, you will be appraised by your line manager.

s.def: To estimate; to conjecture.
To praise; to commend.
To apprise, inform.

ety: From French appréciable. By surface analysis, appreci(ate) + -able.

s.def: Both detectable and at least modestly substantial: large enough to be estimated and to be of practical relevance.
ex: For many people, the benefits of exercise in improving mood and preventing achiness are appreciable.
A grain of musk will scent a drawer for many years, and still lose nothing appreciable of its original weight.
For an appreciable time he did not think of rising from his seat.

s.def: Synonym of detectable.
ex: A small hernia was just barely appreciable upon palpation.

ety: Originated 1645–55; from Medieval Latin appreciātus (“valued or appraised”), later variant of Late Latin appretiātus (“appraised”), the perfect passive participle of appretiō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from a(d) (“toward”) + preti(um) (“price”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix). Cognate to French apprécier. Latin root also origin of English appraise, which has various Romance cognates; see also precious.

s.def: To be grateful or thankful for.

s.def: To view as valuable.

ety: From French appréciation. By surface analysis, appreciate + -ion.

ex: We give to you this trophy as a token of our appreciation of all your years of service.

s.def: Accurate perception; true estimation.
ex: an appreciation of the difficulties before us
an appreciation of colors

s.def: A rise in value.

ety: From Late Middle English apprehenden (“to grasp, take hold of; to comprehend; to learn”), from Old French apprehender (modern French appréhender (“to apprehend; to catch; to dread”)), from Latin apprehendere, adprehendere, the present active infinitive of apprehendō, adprehendō (“to grab, grasp, seize, take; to apprehend, arrest; to comprehend, understand; to embrace, include; to take possession of, obtain, secure”), from ap-, ad- (prefix meaning ‘to’) + prehendō (“to grab, grasp, seize, snatch…

To seize or take (something); to take hold of.
To seize or take (a person) by legal process; to arrest.

He soon returned to the Lowlands, and stayed there till he learned that a considerable body of troops had been sent to apprehend him.

s.def: To feel (something) emotionally.
To learn (something).
To take possession of (something); to seize.

ety: Borrowed from Latin apprehensio, apprehensionis, compare with French appréhension. See apprehend.

ety: From Middle English aprochen, borrowed from Old French aprochier (modern French approcher), from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (a variant of *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + *-kʷe (“suffix forming distributives from interrogatives”)).

ety: From Old French apte, from Latin aptus (“suitable, fitting”). Of a greenish-blue colour.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French aquarelle, from obsolete Italian acquarella (“watercolour”) (later acquarello and acquerello).

ety: Borrowed from Latin aquārius (“water carrier”) (from aqua (“water”) + -arius), calque of Ancient Greek Ὑδροχόος (Hudrokhóos), referring to the Mesopotamian god Ea who was commonly depicted with water pouring from his shoulders or from vases; compare the constellation name in Akkadian 𒀯𒄖𒆷 (ṣinundu), Sumerian 𒀯𒄖𒆷 (ᵐᵘˡGU.LA, “The Great One, Ea”). ety: An unadapted borrowing from French arbitrage, from arbitrer (“to arbitrate”); see arbitrate.

ety: From Middle English arbitrator, from Late Latin arbitrātor, from arbitror.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- Proto-Indo-European *-r Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewsér Proto-Hellenic *auhḗr Ancient Greek ᾱ̓ήρ (āḗr)bor. Latin āera Italian ariabor. English aria From Italian aria, metathesis from Latin āerem, accusative of āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of air.

s.def: A musical piece written typically for a solo voice with orchestral accompaniment in an opera or cantata.

ety: As a 21st century English name from TV and fantasy fiction, explained as "a musical aria". Similar sounding names exist in many languages, e.g. Ariah and Arie from Hebrew, Arya from Sanskrit, and Aria, Dutch short form of Adriana.

s.def: A female given name from English.
ex: Aria Montgomery burrowed her face in her best friend Alison DiLaurentis's lawn.

ety: Uncertain. Rómulo Cúneo Vidal said that the word comes from Aymara ari (crag) + iqui (place to sleep). Manuel A. Quiroga said that the word comes from ari (phylum) + aka (tip). Carlos Auza Arce said that it comes from ari (hill) + acca (neighboring).

s.def: A commune and port city, the capital of the province of Arica, Chile.
A province in northern Chile.

s.def: Very dry.
ex: The cake was arid.

s.def: Describing a very dry climate. Typically defined as less than 25 cm or 10 inches of rainfall annually.
ex: Deserts are known for being arid.
And because this part of Utah is arid, the geologic landscape is fully revealed with very little vegetation to hide it, faults and all.

s.def: Devoid of value.
ex: The millionaire viewed his gift as arid.
Such occupations might have seemed arid to those who did not possess the intellect to appreciate their subtleties.

ety: From Latin Aries, from aries (“ram”), calque of Ancient Greek Κριός (Kriós), calque of Akkadian 𒅈𒌺𒊑𒈨 (immeru, “sheep”).

s.def: A constellation of the zodiac traditionally figured in the shape of a ram.
ex: The Bull, being gall’d, gave Aries such a knock / That down fell both the Ram’s horns in the court.

s.def: The zodiac sign for the ram, ruled by Mars and covering March 20 – April 20 (tropical astrology) or April 15 – May 15 (sidereal astrology).

ety: From Middle English ariȝt, ariht, from Old English āriht (“aright, properly”), from earlier *an riht, on riht (“rightly”), corresponding to a- + right.

s.def: Rightly, correctly; in the right way or form.
ex: The great service which he rendered to science was that he put the right questions ; it was not that he answered them aright.
"Well, gentlemen, have I read you the riddle aright, or is there any point which you would query?"

s.def: To or on the right-hand side.
ex: Once more away! and now The long descent is seen, A long, long, narrow path. Ice rocks aright, and hills of snow, Aleft the giddy precipice.

s.def: To make right; put right; arrange or treat properly.

ety: From Middle English arisen, from Old English ārīsan (“to arise, get up; rise; spring from, originate; spring up, ascend”), from Proto-Germanic *uzrīsaną (“to rise up, arise”), equivalent to a- + rise. Cognate with Scots arise, aryse (“to arise, rise up, come into existence”), Middle Low German errīsen (“to stand up, arise”), Old High German irrīsan (“to rise up, fall”), Gothic 𐌿𐍂𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (urreisan, “to arise”). Eclipsed Middle English sourden, sorden, borrowed from Old French sordre, sour…

s.def: get up, stand up
To come up from a lower to a higher position.
ex: to arise from a kneeling posture

s.def: To come up from one's bed or place of repose; to get up.
ex: He arose early in the morning.

s.def: To spring up; to come into action, being, or notice; to become operative, sensible, or visible; to begin to act a part; to present itself.
ex: A cloud arose and covered the sun.
A new challenge will arise every time you think you've solved the last one.
The issue began to arise when the team members couldn't agree on the plan.

s.def: Arising, rising.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French aristocratie, from Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā, “the rule of the best“, that is, “the best-born”, “nobility”), from ἄριστος (áristos, “best, noblest”) + -κρατίᾱ (-kratíā), from κράτος (krátos, “power, rule”). By surface analysis, aristo- + -cracy.

s.def: The nobility, or the hereditary ruling class.
ex: That, then, which is called aristocracy in some countries and nobility in others arose out of the governments founded upon conquest.

s.def: Government by such a class, or a state with such a government.
A class of people considered (not normally universally) superior to others.

ety: From French aristocrate (“aristocrat”), attested once in the 16th century but recoined in the Revolutionary era, from aristocratie (“aristocracy”), from Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατία (aristokratía), from ἄριστος (áristos, “best”) (compare Old English ar) + κράτος (krátos, “rule”). By surface analysis, aristo- + -crat.

s.def: One of the aristocracy, nobility, or people of rank in a community; one of a ruling class; a noble (originally in Revolutionary France).
ex: The remains of a Roman aristocrat have been unearthed by archaeologists in northern England.
Magazines kept aristocrats on the payroll to facilitate access to jet-set playgrounds like Corfu and Mustique.

s.def: A proponent of aristocracy; an advocate of aristocratic government.
A cipher in which the original punctuation and spacing are retained.

ety: Cockney rhyming slang for bottle, itself shortened from bottle and glass, Cockney rhyming slang for arse.

s.def: A bottle.

ety: Via Latin Aristotelēs from Ancient Greek Ἀριστοτέλης (Aristotélēs).

s.def: A male given name.

Number theory.

ex: arithmetic geometry

ex: arithmetic progression

ety: Uncertain. Possibly from O'odham alĭ ṣonak (literally “small spring”) (traditionally through the Spanish intermediary form Arizonac; compare modern Arizona), a name initially applied to an area around a silver-mining camp in Sonora. Alternatively, perhaps from Basque haritz ona (literally “good oak”), as the area had many Basque herders, and a descendant of them established the ranchería of Arizona (circa 1735) in Sonora. Suggestions of derivation from *arizuma, supposedly a Nahuatl word meanin…

s.def: a state of the United States of America
A state in the southwestern United States, established 1912. Capital: Phoenix.
Ellipsis of University of Arizona.
ex: Videos on social media appear to show Arizona fans chanting “F**k the Mormons” after the 96-95 loss.

s.def: A territory of the southwest Confederate (1862–1865) and United States of America (1863–1912), with its capitals at Tucson, Prescott, and Phoenix.
A department of the northwest Second Mexican Empire (1863–1865), with its capital at Altar.
A unisex given name.
Arizona Beverage Company, which sells its products under the name AriZona.
Several places named for the state or territory.
A surname.

ety: From Middle English arke, from Old English earc, ærc, from Latin arca (“chest, box, coffer”), from arceō (“to enclose”).

s.def: The ship built by Noah to save his family and a collection of animals from the deluge; Noah's ark.
A large box with a flat lid.
ex: Then said he, "Your child is at home in the inner bedroom in a new cradle behind the ark."

s.def: Something affording protection; safety, shelter, refuge.
ex: the Ark of Bukhara

s.def: The body as a vessel.
ex: Like her I go; I cannot stay; ⁠I leave this mortal ark behind, A weight of nerves without a mind, And leave the cliffs, and haste away […]

s.def: A spacious type of boat with a flat bottom.
ex: Some seventy or seventy-five arks were permanently located on McLeod's Lake and between 110 and 125 people lived in them.

s.def: The Ark of the Covenant.
A decorated cabinet at the front of a synagogue, in which Torah scrolls are kept.
The sacred container, a gold-plated wooden chest, of the two tablets of law (the Ten Commandments) given to Moses by the Hebrew God.

ety: From the name of the Arkansas River, from French Arcansas, a (plural) designation of either a Siouan tribe or the Quapaw. This designation is sometimes claimed to derive from a Quapaw word *akakaze (“land of downriver people”) or a Lakota/Dakota word *akakaze (“people of the south wind”); more likely, it derives from a Siouan ethnonym cognate to Kansa (whence also the name of the state of Kansas).

s.def: American state
A state in the South Central region of the United States. Capital and largest city: Little Rock.

A river in the United States, rising in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado, and flowing generally southeast over 1,400 miles through Kansas, Oklahoma and Arkansas, where it joins the Mississippi in Desha County.
A surname.

ety: Borrowed from Russian Арха́нгельск (Arxángelʹsk).

s.def: city in Russia
An oblast in northwestern Russia.
A city, the administrative center of Arkhangelsk Oblast, in northwestern Russia, on the White Sea.

ex: She stood with her right arm extended and her palm forward to indicate “Stop!”

s.def: A weapon.

s.def: To take up weapons; to arm oneself.
ex: The sergeant sent out an order to arm the team for the next mission.
Are you arming, comrade Atheists? Are you arming for the fray?

s.def: A limb, or locomotive or prehensile organ, of an invertebrate animal.
ex: the arms of an octopus

s.def: The part of a piece of clothing that covers the arm.
ex: […] one arm of this jacket streamed behind him like the broidered arm of a huzzar’s surcoat.
[…] he noticed that a dark stain had appeared under the arm of her grey silk dress.
Samad made a grab for the boy and caught him by the arm of his shirt.

s.def: A long, narrow, more or less rigid part of an object extending from the main part or centre of the object, such as the armrest of an armchair, a crane, a pair of spectacles or a pair of compasses.
ex: The robot arm reached out and placed the part on the assembly line.
I accidentally sat on my glasses and bent one of the arms.

s.def: A bay or inlet off a main body of water.

s.def: A branch of an organization.
ex: the cavalry arm of the military service

s.def: With arms linked together; with arms around each other's shoulder or waist. (of two or more people)
ex: The two friends walked along arm in arm.
[…] Laurie came running down stairs, and brought up with a start of surprise at the sight of Jo arm in arm with his redoubtable grandfather.

s.def: In collusion, in concert (with someone).
The length of a person's outstretched arms, measured from the fingertips of the two middle fingers. See also fathom
A strength sport with two participants, in which each participant grips the other's hand and tries to pin the other's arm onto a surface.

Alternative letter-case form of Armageddon.

ety: The proper noun is from Middle English Hermagedon, from Old English Ermagedon, from Late Latin Harmagedōn, from Ancient Greek Ἁρμαγεδών (Harmagedṓn), used in the New Testament of the Bible (see the quotations) to render Hebrew הַר מְגִדּוֹ (har megído, “Mount Megiddo, the place where the final battle before the Last Judgment is predicted to occur”) from הַר (har, “mountain”) + מְגִידּוֹ (megído, “Megiddo or Meggidon, ancient city of Canaan”). The battle itself.

ety: From Latin armāmentum, from armō (“to arm”).

s.def: A body of forces equipped for war.
All the cannon and small arms collectively, with their equipments, belonging to a ship or a fortification.
Any equipment for resistance.
The process of building up military capacity.

ety: From Latin armāmentārium (“arsenal”), from armāmenta (“tools, equipment, rigging”) + -ārium. By surface analysis, armament + -arium.

s.def: All of the equipment available for carrying out a task, especially all the equipment used by a physician in the practice of medicine.
ex: The most important tool in the photographer's armamentarium for evaluating the range of possibilities at each site is his or her feet.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French armature, from Latin armātūra (“armour”). Doublet of armor and armure.

s.def: A detachment of soldiers; soldiers collectively.
Armor, such as a suit of armor, weapons and other military equipment.
The art of using arms and armour in combat; skill at arms; a mode or manner of armed combat.
The rotating part of an electric motor or dynamo, which mostly consists of coils of wire (the winding) around a metal core.
The moving part in an electromechanical device like a loudspeaker or a buzzer.
A piece of soft steel or iron that connects the poles of a magnet, to preserve its strength by forming a circuit.
A supporting framework in a sculpture.
A kinematic chain (a system of bones or rigid bodies connected by joints) that is used to pose and deform models, often character models.
A protective organ, structure, or covering of an animal or plant, for defense or offense, like claws, teeth, thorns, or the shell of a turtle.
Any apparatus for defence.

A town in that province.
A city in Krasnodar Krai, Russia.

ety: From arm + band.

One of a pair of inflatable plastic bands, normally worn on the upper arms, to help the wearer (often a child) float in water and learn to swim.
A band worn around the arm of the captain of a team.

The military forces of a nation, such as the army, navy, air force, marines, and sometimes, coastguard or border guard, which are tasked with the defence of the nation and its citizens, if necessary through use of deadly force.
ex: What dictators fear most is losing the support of the armed forces, and when this happens, it's as if a ferocious beast has lost its teeth.

s.def: A theft where the thieves are armed with weapons.

Ancient kingdom in the Armenian Highland southeast of Black Sea and southwest of Caspian Sea; area now divided between Turkey, Republic of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Iran.

ety: From Armenia + -an.

s.def: The language of Armenia and the Armenian people, whose older stages are Old Armenian and Middle Armenian.
A branch of Indo-European languages, which includes the various stages of the Armenian language.

ety: Unknown. Although the snake melon has been cultivated since antiquity, the term mentioning Armenia originated in the US c. the 1950s.

s.def: Cucumis melo var. flexuosus, a long, slender variety of muskmelon which resembles a cucumber in taste and inner appearance.
One of the 15 Soviet Socialist Republics that made up the former Soviet Union (1920-1991, name changed in 1990). Became independent as the Republic of Armenia in 1991, after the collapse of the USSR.

An instrument consisting of graduated metal circles used to represent the motions of celestial bodies around the earth.

ety: From Late Latin armistitium, from Latin arma (“arms, weapons”) + sistēre (from sistō (“to halt, stand still”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand up”)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns). Alternative letter-case form of Armistice (“the armistice agreement signed between the Allies and Germany on 11 November 1918 to end World War I; (by extension) the end of World War I”).

ex: The arms of England are: gules, three lions passant guardant or.

ety: From Middle English aside, asyde, a-side, oside, from Middle English on side, from Old English on sīdan (literally “on (the) side (of)”), equivalent to a- + side. Compare beside.

The sense referring to books of maps comes from the Atlas of Mercator, which he named thus in honor of Atlas, who was supposed to be skillful in astronomy and the doctrine of the sphere. The sense referring to the vertebra reflects that the spine carries the globe of the cranium (the neck carries the head).
