English -osis English avitaminosis From a- + vitamin + -osis.

s.def: Any disease which is caused by vitamin deficiency.

ety: Borrowed from Latin American Spanish avocado, from the earlier aguacate, which comes from Classical Nahuatl āhuacatl (“avocado”). Doublet of abacate. Compare aguacatillo, avocadillo. The first mention can be found in a catalogue of Jamaican plants in 1696.

s.def: The avocado tree, Persea americana, of the laurel family.
The large, usually yellowish-green or black, savory fruit of the avocado tree.
A dark chartreuse color, like the color of the skin of an avocado.
ex: It was exactly the same as my bathroom. Same cork floor, same avocado bathroom set.

s.def: Of a dull yellowish-green colour.

ety: From Latin āvocātiō (“a distraction”), from āvocō (“to call off, distract”).

s.def: A calling away; a diversion.
A hobby or recreational or leisure pursuit.
ex: But yield who will to their separation, My object in living is to unite My avocation and my vocation As my two eyes make one in sight.
Gardening is a wholesome avocation that encourages appreciation for nature and concern for the preservation and enhancement of our environment.

s.def: That which calls one away from one's regular employment or vocation.
Pursuits; duties; affairs which occupy one's time; usual employment; vocation.
The calling of a case from an inferior to a superior court.

ety: From French avocette, from Italian avocetta.

s.def: Any of four species of wading birds in the genus Recurvirostra, with long, slender recurved bills, long legs, and webbed feet.

ety: Named after Italian physicist Amedeo Avogadro (1776–1856).

s.def: The number of elementary entities (atoms or molecules) comprising one mole of a given substance, being precisely 6.02214076 × 10²³. Formerly defined as the number of atoms present in 12 grams of isotopically pure carbon-12.

ety: From Middle English avoiden, from Anglo-Norman avoider, Old French esvuidier (“to empty out”), from es- + vuidier, from Vulgar Latin *vocitāre < Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately related to Latin vacuus. Displaced native Old English forbūgan (literally “to bend away from”).

s.def: To keep away from; to keep clear of; to stay away from.
ex: I try to avoid the company of gamblers.

s.def: To defeat or evade; to invalidate.
to try not to be hit; to give way
To try not to meet or communicate with (a person); to shun.
To stay out of the way of (something harmful).
ex: I avoided the slap easily.
One town was flooded from the storm, while the other town avoided the storm.

s.def: To try not to do something or to have something happen.
ex: Then he realized, by the immobility of the other children and by the way they avoided looking at him, that it was he who was selected for punishment.

s.def: To make empty; to clear.
To make void, to annul; to refute (especially a contract).
ex: […] how can those graunts of the Kings be avoyded, without wronging of those lords, which had those lands and lordships given them?

s.def: To emit or throw out; to void.
To leave, evacuate; to leave as empty, to withdraw or come away from.

ant: take the bull by the horns

ety: From Middle English avoir de pois, aver de peis, haburdy poyse, haburdepays, haburdepeyse, from Old French aveir + de + peis (“asset of weight”), influenced by Middle French avoir + du + pois; compare French poids (“weight”).

s.def: The official system of weights used in the UK between 1856 and 1963. It had been the customary system in London since 1300.
The official system of weights used in the USA between 1866 and 1959.
Weight; heaviness.
ex: It seems humanly reasonable that the three of us can woman-handle a mere man of your elderly and insulting avoirdupois.

s.def: Merchandise.

ety: From Old French avouchier, from Latin advocāre. Doublet of advocate, advoke, and avow.

s.def: To declare freely and openly; to assert.
ex: If this which he avouches does appear, There is nor flying hence nor tarrying here.

s.def: To acknowledge deliberately; to admit; to confess; to sanction.
To confirm or verify, to affirm the validity of.
To appeal to; to cite or claim as authority.
ex: And for proofe of their opinion they avouch many successions of authorities that no fee simple should passe before the condition performed.

s.def: evidence; declaration
ex: Before my God, I might not this believe Without the sensible and true avouch Of mine own eyes.

ety: From Middle English avowen, from Old French avouer, from Latin advocare (“to call to, call upon, hence to call as a witness, defender, patron, or advocate”), from ad (“to”) + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of advoke, avouch, and advocate. Not related to vow.

s.def: To declare openly and boldly, as something believed to be right; to own, acknowledge or confess frankly.
ex: […] in 1786, and for some period later, there were few, if any, prominent Americans, who avowed themselves in favor of broadly democratic systems.

s.def: To bind or devote by a vow.
ex: No man may halewe and avowe the firste gendrid thingis that perteynen to the Lord, whether it is oxe, whether scheep, tho ben the Lordis part.

s.def: To acknowledge and justify, as an act done. See avowry.
ex: avow himself the accomplice of his crimes

s.def: avowal

ety: From Latin avulsio from a- + vellō.

s.def: The loss or separation of a body part, either by surgery or due to trauma.
ex: Immediately observable were avulsion of several teeth and extensive lacerations and bruising to the face.

s.def: An abrupt change in the course of a river, typically from one channel to another.
Movement of soil during a flood, or during a change in the course of a river, especially when a resulting change of land ownership is involved.

ety: From Medieval Latin avunculāris, from Classical Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -āris (“-ar”).

s.def: In the manner of an uncle, pertaining to an uncle.
Kind, genial, benevolent, or tolerant.
ex: But Jackson had an avuncular feeling for the two younger men and he assumed it was his duty to pull them from their gloom.
A man with such a nice, avuncular personality would not blow up the world.

ety: From Classical Latin avuncul(us) (“maternal uncle”) + -ate.

s.def: The relationship between a man and his sister's children, generally her sons.
Among certain tribal peoples, for example, the Korowai, a special relationship between a man and a maternal uncle, and the mutual responsibilities between them.

ety: From Middle English awaiten, from Old Northern French awaitier (“to lie in wait for, watch, observe”), originally especially with a hostile sense; itself from a- (“to”) + waitier (“to watch”). More at English wait.

s.def: To wait for.
ex: I await your reply to my letter.
Betwixt these rocky pillars Gabriel sat, / Chief of the angelic guards, awaiting night;
In love, however, women are brave. How many clamber over rooftops of houses and palaces, and are still doing it, when their lovers await them!

s.def: To expect.
To be in store for; to be ready or in waiting for.
ex: Glorious rewards await the good in heaven; eternal suffering awaits mortal sinners in hell.
O Eve, some further change awaits us nigh.

s.def: To serve or attend; to wait on, wait upon.
To watch, observe.
To wait; to stay in waiting.
ex: These are exotic lands where great adventures await.

s.def: A waiting for; ambush.
Watching, watchfulness, suspicious observation.
ex: For all that night, the whyles the Prince did rest […] He watcht in close awayt with weapons prest […]

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ud-s-? Proto-Indo-European *h₂u-s-? Proto-Germanic *uz- Proto-West Germanic *uʀ- Old English ar- Old English ā- Proto-Indo-European *weǵ-der. Proto-Germanic *wakaną Proto-West Germanic *wakan Old English wacan Old English āwacan Middle English awaken Middle English awake English awake From Middle English awake, a shortened form of awaken (“awakened, awake”), past participle of Middle English awaken (“to awaken”). See verb below. Compare Saterland Frisian woak…

s.def: Not asleep; conscious.
Alert, aware.
ex: They were awake to the possibility of a decline in sales.
The Baker was a two-handed hitter, and seemed perfectly awake to the business before him.

s.def: To cause (somebody) to stop sleeping.
To become conscious after having slept.
To make aware of something.
To excite or to stir up something latent.
To rouse from a state of inaction or dormancy.
To come out of a state of inaction or dormancy.
ex: 1867-1879, Edward Augustus Freeman, The History of the Norman Conquest of England The national spirit again awoke.
Awake to righteousness, and sin not.

s.def: Used in a phrasal verb: to awake to (“to become awake of something and its possibile effects or results.”).
ex: It took her some time to awake to the dangers of her situation.

s.def: Used in a phrasal verb: to awake to (“to be roused from one's sleep, due to a noise or other stimulus.”).
ex: this morning, I awoke to the sound of my neighbor's barking dog.

ety: From Middle English awakenen or awaknen, from Old English awæcnan or awæcnian, from a- plus wæcnan or wæcnian.

s.def: To cause to become awake.
To stop sleeping; awake.
ex: Each morning he awakens with a smile on his face.

s.def: transitive: to cause to become conscious
To bring into action (something previously dormant); to stimulate.
ex: Awaken your entrepreneurial spirit!
We hope to awaken your interest in our programme.
He tries to awaken in them self-respect and reverence for their own spiritual culture.

s.def: Of something previously dormant, to become active.
To call to a sense of sin.
past participle of awake
To cause to become aware.
To become aware.
ex: I suddenly awoke to the possibilities of the new invention.

ety: From Middle English awarden, from Anglo-Norman awarder, from Medieval Latin *exwardare, from Latin ex (“out”) + Medieval Latin wardare, guardare (“to observe, regard, guard”); see ward, guard, regard.

s.def: A trophy or medal; something that denotes an accomplishment, especially in a competition. A prize or honor based on merit.
A judgment, sentence, or final decision. Specifically: The decision of arbitrators in a case submitted.
The paper containing the decision of arbitrators; that which is warded.
Funding that has been granted for the conduct of a research project.
A negotiated set of employment conditions and minimum wages for a particular trade or industry; an industrial award.
ex: Employees whose pay is set by ‘award only’ are those who have their pay set by an award, and who are not paid more than the award rate of pay.

s.def: To determine; to make or grant an award.
To give (an award).
ex: Four or five of these medals are awarded every year.
He was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature.

s.def: To give (a person) an award.
ex: He was awarded with the Nobel Prize for Literature.

s.def: To give by sentence or judicial determination; to assign or apportion, after careful regard to the nature of the case.
ex: The arbitrators awarded damages to the complainant.
To review / The wrongful sentence, and award a new.
Power to award compensation

s.def: (in an examination) To give marks for a correct answer.
ex: Do not award marks for data from previous questions.

s.def: A ceremony, with a theme, at which awards are given out.

ety: Inherited from Middle English aware, iwar, iware, ywar, from Old English ġewær (“aware”), from Proto-West Germanic *gawar, from Proto-Germanic *waraz (“aware, cautious”), from Proto-Indo-European *worós (“attentive”), from *wer- (“to heed; watch out”). Cognate with Dutch gewaar, German gewahr, Danish var, Swedish var, Icelandic varr.

s.def: Vigilant or on one's guard against danger or difficulty.
ex: Stay aware! Don't let your guard down.

s.def: Conscious or having knowledge of something; awake.
ex: Are you aware of what is being said about you?
Gotta get going. I wasn’t aware that it was already so late.

s.def: To make (someone) aware of something.

ety: Etymology tree English aware Proto-Germanic *-in- Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ti Proto-Germanic *-ōną Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English awareness From aware + -ness.

s.def: The state or level of consciousness where sense data can be confirmed by an observer.
ex: I gradually passed from sleep to full awareness.

s.def: The state or quality of being aware of something.
ex: raise awareness of a topic
The awareness of one type of idea naturally fosters an awareness of another idea
With the growing awareness of climate change, congestion, and regional inequality, rail transport has re-emerged as a solution.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Hellenic *ə- Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-)der. English a- Proto-Indo-European *wed- Proto-Indo-European *-sḱéti Proto-Indo-European *wodsḱéti Proto-Germanic *waskaną Proto-West Germanic *waskan Old English wascan Middle English wasshen English wash English awash From a- + wash.

s.def: Washed by the waves or tide (of a rock or strip of shore, or of an anchor, etc., when flush with the surface of the water, so that the waves break over it); covered with water.
ex: The former rock is awash at low water […]
The deck was continually awash with the sea which came inboard over the rail and through the scuppers.
but the river’s in flood / and the roads are awash / and the bridges break up / in the panic of loss.

s.def: Covered, overspread (with or in something).
ex: Tonight, his mind was awash with visions:
[…] the whole country’s awash in guns and Bibles,
THE LIQUID SAMURAI ROSE, AWASH IN THE MIRROR'S MAGIC.

ety: From Middle English away, awey, awei, oway, o wey, on way, from Old English āweġ, onweġ (“away”), originally on weġ (“on one's way; onward; on”), equivalent to a- (“on”) + way. Cognate with Scots awa, away (“away”), Old Frisian aweg, awei (“away”), Saterland Frisian wäch, wääge (“away”), Dutch weg (“away”), German weg (“away”), Danish væk (“away”), Swedish i väg (“away; off; along”).

s.def: From a place, hence.
ex: He went away on vacation.

s.def: Aside; off; in another direction.
ex: I tried to approach him, but he turned away.

s.def: Aside, so as to discard something.
ex: throw away, chuck away, toss away

s.def: At a stated distance in time or space.
ex: Christmas is only two weeks away.

s.def: In or to something's usual or proper storage place.
ex: I'll dry the dishes and you put them away.
Please file away these documents.

s.def: In or to a secure or out-of-the-way place.
ex: The jewels were locked away in the safe.
He was shut away in the castle tower for six months.

s.def: From a state or condition of being; out of existence.
ex: fade away, die away
I'll sleep the rest of the day away/out and, hopefully, I'll manage to sleep this hangover off/away.

s.def: So as to remove or use up something.
ex: The weather has worn away the inscription, and it is no longer legible.
Please wipe away this spilled drink.
He gambled his inheritance away, while I bargained away my birthrights

s.def: Come away; go away; take away.
ex: Away! Be gone! And don't let me see you round here again!
1933+, Fran Striker, The Lone Ranger, WXYZ-AM Hi-yo Silver, away!

s.def: On; in continuance; without intermission or delay.
ex: She's been in her room all day, working away at her computer.

ety: From Middle English aw, awe, agh, awȝe, borrowed from Old Norse agi, from Proto-Germanic *agaz (“terror, dread”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʰ- (“to be upset, afraid”). Displaced native Middle English eye, eyȝe, ayȝe, eȝȝe, from Old English ege, æge (“fear, terror, dread”), from the same Proto-Germanic root.

s.def: A feeling of fear and reverence.
A feeling of amazement.
Power to inspire awe.
To inspire fear and reverence in.
To control by inspiring dread.
A bucket (blade) attached to water wheels.

ety: From a- + weather; distantly cognate in structure to German Gewitter.

s.def: On the weather side, or toward the wind; in the direction from which the wind blows (See upwind)
ex: Helm aweather!

ety: From awe + -some; compare earlier awful and Middle English eiful (“inducing fright or terror, terrible”), from Old English eġeful (“fearful; inspiring awe”). The oldest meaning of awesome is of “something which inspires awe”, but the word is now also a common colloquial expression. It was originally so used in the United States, where it had featured strikingly in the 1970 film Tora! Tora! Tora!, as used by Japan's Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto to describe the "awesome" industrial potential of the U…

s.def: Causing awe or terror; inspiring wonder or excitement.
ex: The waterfall in the middle of the rainforest was an awesome sight.
The tsunami was awesome in its destructive power.
Certainly it is awesome to think of a nation that brings its powers of persuasion against a woman's right to conceive.

s.def: Excellent, exciting, remarkable.
ex: That was awesome!
Awesome, dude!
Awesome! Totally awesome! All right, Hamilton!

ety: From Middle English agheful, awfull, auful, aȝefull, equivalent to awe + -ful. Compare Old English eġeful, eġefull (“terrifying; awful”). The “very bad” sense is a pejorative semantic shift from the original sense of “awe-inspiring”.

s.def: Causing fear or horror; appalling, terrible.
ex: At our old pastimes in the hall ⁠We gambol’d, making vain pretence ⁠Of gladness, with an awful sense Of one mute Shadow watching all.

s.def: Very bad.
ex: The smell of my socks is awful.
We saw such an awful film last night that we left the theater before the end.

s.def: Exceedingly great; usually applied intensively.
ex: I have learnt an awful amount today.
“[…] I cook a lot. I make an awful lot of food. Jason thinks I must be cooking for an army sometimes,” she says, […]

s.def: Awe-inspiring; filling with profound reverence or respect; profoundly impressive.
ex: God ought not to be commixed in our actions, but with awful reverence, and an attention full of honour and respect.
And then she stopped, and stood as if in awe / (For sleep is awful)[…].

s.def: Struck or filled with awe or reverence.
Terror-stricken.
Prone to a particular temptation.
ex: "It's her imagination, that's what it is," Millie said. "She's awful for imagining things, Wilfred agreed with me."
Tommy was just an awful man for the paper - couldn't get enough of the stuff! He'd have had the very Yellow Pages down him!

s.def: Awfully; dreadfully; terribly.
ex: The race was run, and the dog ran "awful".

s.def: Very, extremely.
ex: That's an awful big house.
She seemed awful nice when I met her yesterday.
He was blubbering away something awful.

ety: From Old English āne (“(for) a”) hwīle (“while”).

s.def: For some time; for a short time.
ex: Sit with me awhile.
Take two cupfuls of rolled oats, put in bread pan, turn on four cupfuls of boiling water, stir for awhile.
Engine No. 18 went off into a shed to rest awhile, and No. 7, a precisely similar one, backed on to the train in her place.

s.def: In the meantime; during an implicit ongoing process.
ex: Can I get you a drink awhile?

ety: From a- + whirl.

s.def: Whirling.
ex: My mind was awhirl with new ideas.
golden leaves awhirl in the autumn breeze
The music rippled and ran and the dancers danced till the hall was awhirl with the rhythm of their dancing,

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep Proto-Indo-European *-o Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- Proto-Indo-European *h₂époh₃kʷos Proto-Germanic *abuhaz Old Norse ǫfugrder. Middle English awke English awk Proto-Indo-European *wert-der. Proto-Germanic *wardaz Old English -weard English -ward English awkward From awk (“odd, clumsy”) + -ward. Compare Middle English aukeward (“in the wrong direction”).

s.def: Lacking dexterity in the use of the hands, or of instruments.
ex: John was awkward at performing the trick. He'll have to practice to improve.

s.def: Not easily managed or effected; embarrassing.
ex: That was an extremely awkward moment. Everyone was watching.
An awkward silence had fallen.

s.def: Perverse; adverse; difficult to handle.
ex: He's a right awkward chap.
These cabinets are going to be very awkward when we move.
Clearing up rock and fallen vegetation at such an awkward site required a team of specialist geoengineers.

s.def: Lacking social skills, or uncomfortable with social interaction.
ex: I'm very awkward at parties.
Things got awkward when my boss tried a cheesy pick-up line on me.

s.def: Someone or something that is awkward.
ex: That is a way to make awkwards. And it's not fun to hang out with awkwards more than once.

ety: From Middle English aul, alle, al, from Old English æl, from Proto-West Germanic *al, from Proto-Germanic *alaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ólos. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Äil (“awl”), Dutch aal (“awl”), German Low German Ahl (“awl”), German Ahle (“awl”), Icelandic alur (“awl”). Spelling was influenced by the Old English synonym awel, awul (“awl”), from Proto-West Germanic *ahwal, from Proto-Germanic *ahwalaz (“fork, hook”), of unknown origin. Doublet of elsen.

s.def: A pointed instrument for piercing small holes, as in leather or wood; used by shoemakers, saddlers, cabinetmakers, etc. The blade is differently shaped and pointed for different uses, as in the brad awl, saddler's awl, shoemaker's awl, etc.
ex: He dressed himself in some old ragged clothes, and took a tame white bear, which he had, with him, as well as an awl, some pitch, and twine.

s.def: Any of various hesperiid butterflies.

ety: Inherited from Middle English aw(u)ne, agune, from Old Norse ǫgn (compare Danish avne), from Proto-Germanic *aganō, *ahanō (“chaff”) (compare Old English agnu, Dutch agen, German Ahne, Agen), from Proto-Indo-European *aḱanā (compare Latin agna (“ear of wheat”), Lithuanian ašni̇̀s (“edge, blade”), Czech osina, Ancient Greek ἄκαινα (ákaina, “spike, prick”), ἄκανος (ákanos, “pine-thistle”), Sanskrit अशनि (aśáni, “thunderbolt, arrow tip”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). More at edge.

s.def: The bristle or beard of barley, oats, grasses, etc., or any similar bristlelike appendage; arista.

ety: 1615-25 (nautical sense only); from *awn + -ing, reduction of Middle French auvans (“sloping roof”), from Old French anvant (1180), from Gaulish *an(de)bannā (“eaves”) (compare Occitan ambans (“parapet”)), form of *ande- (intensive prefix) (compare Welsh an-, Old Irish ind-) + *bandā (“horn; peak”) (compare Welsh ban, Irish beann).

s.def: A rooflike cover, usually of canvas, extended over or before any place as a shelter from the sun, rain, or wind.
That part of the poop deck which is continued forward beyond the bulkhead of the cabin.

ety: From Middle English awry, awrie. By surface analysis, a- + wry.

s.def: Obliquely, crookedly; askew.
Perversely, improperly.
Turned or twisted toward one side; crooked, distorted, out of place; wry.
ex: The frame was awry.

s.def: Wrong or distorted; perverse, amiss, off course
ex: There is something awry with this story.

ety: From Middle English ax, axe, ex, from Old English æx (“axe”), from Proto-West Germanic *akusi (“axe”), from Proto-Germanic *akwisī (“axe”), probably from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷsih₂ (“axe”), from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”). Cognate with Scots aix (“axe”), Dutch aks (“axe”), German Axt (“axe”), Danish økse (“axe”), Faroese, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk øks (“axe”), Icelandic öxi (“axe”), Swedish yxa (“axe”), Latin ascia (“axe, mason's trowel”).

s.def: A tool for felling trees or chopping wood etc. consisting of a heavy head flattened to a blade on one side, and a handle attached to it.
An ancient weapon consisting of a head that has one or two blades and a long handle.
A dismissal or rejection.
ex: His girlfriend/boss/schoolmaster gave him the axe.

s.def: A drastic reduction or cutback.
ex: the Beeching Axe
The tractor plant is slated for the axe.
I had a job in the great North Woods Workin' as a cook for a spell But I never did like it all that much And one day the axe just fell

s.def: A gigging musician's particular instrument, especially a guitar in rock music or a saxophone in jazz.
A position, interest, or reason in buying and selling stock, often with ulterior motives.
ex: A financial dealer has an axe in a stock that his buyers don't know about, giving him an advantage in making the most profit.

s.def: To fell or chop with an axe.
To lay off, terminate or drastically reduce, especially in a rough or ruthless manner; to cancel.
ex: The government announced its plans to axe public spending.
The broadcaster axed the series because far fewer people than expected watched it.
He got axed in the last round of firings.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ-? Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs-der. Proto-Italic *aksis Latin axisbor. English axis Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English axial From axis + -al.

s.def: Relating to, resembling, or situated on an axis
ex: The axial asymmetry of Mercury's inertia ellipsoid may result in a torque that counterbalances the tidal torque

s.def: Belonging to the axis of the body, or to the axis of any appendage or organ
ex: the axial skeleton
the axial bones

s.def: In the same direction as the axis, parallel to the axis.
ex: The secondary xylem usually consists of axial and radial elements.

s.def: Oriented parallel to the axis running through the centre of a cyclohexane ring, as opposed to equatorial. See Axial bond.
A flight feather that appears between the primaries and secondaries on some birds.
A plane parallel to the surface of a tooth.

ety: From Latin axilla. Doublet of axilla.

s.def: The angle or point of divergence between the upper side of a branch, leaf, or petiole, and the stem or branch from which it springs.
ex: Near-synonyms: crotch, fork

ety: Borrowed from Latin axilla (“side, armpit”). Doublet of axil.

s.def: The armpit, or the cavity beneath the junction of the arm and shoulder.
The area that is located posterior to the transscutal articulation and anterior to the scutoscutellar suture.
Alternative form of axil.

ety: Alteration by association with -ary of the French axillaire (“of the axilla”), itself an alteration of the earlier forms aisselliere and aissellaire, both from the assumed Latin etymon *axillāris, from axilla (“armpit”), diminutive form of the assumed *axula.

s.def: Of or pertaining to the axilla or armpit.
Situated in, or rising from, an axil; relating to an axil.
Alternative form of axillar.

ety: From Ancient Greek ἄξιος (áxios, “worthy”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”).

s.def: The study of value(s), as regards origin, nature, functions, types, and interrelations; value theory.
The particular value-theory of a philosopher, school of thought, etc.
ex: In his axiology, G. E. Moore maintains that "good" is the name of a simple, indefinable quality.

ety: From Middle French axiome in the 15th century, from Latin axiōma (“axiom; principle”), from Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma, “that which is thought to fit, a requisite, that which a pupil is required to know beforehand, a self-evident principle”), from ἀξιόω (axióō, “to think fit or worthy, to require, to demand”), from ἄξιος (áxios, “fit, worthy”, literally “weighing as much as; of like value”), from ἄγω (ágō, “to weigh (down)”).

s.def: A seemingly self-evident or necessary truth which is based on assumption; a principle or proposition which cannot actually be proved or disproved.
ex: Near-synonyms: given, facticity
Any publicity, runs the axiom, is good publicity.

s.def: A fundamental assumption that serves as a basis for deduction of theorems; a postulate (sometimes distinguished from postulates as being universally applicable, whereas postulates are particular to a certain science or context).
ex: Holonym: formal system
Near-synonyms: given, facticity

s.def: An established principle in some artistic practice or science that is universally received.
ex: The axioms of political economy cannot be considered absolute truths.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ-? Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs-der. Proto-Italic *aksis Latin axisbor. English axis Borrowed from Latin axis (“axle, axis”) in the 16th century. Via Latin cognate with ala, aisle, atelier. Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- cognate with inherited English axle and borrowed axo-, axon.

s.def: An imaginary line around which an object spins (an axis of rotation) or is symmetrically arranged (an axis of symmetry).
ex: The Earth rotates once a day on its axis

s.def: A fixed one-dimensional figure, such as a line or arc, with an origin and orientation and such that its points are in one-to-one correspondence with a set of numbers; an axis forms part of the basis of a space or is used to position and locate data in a graph (a coordinate axis)
The second cervical vertebra of the spine
An imaginary, visualized plane separating two morphologically similar parts of an organism
A form of classification and descriptions of mental disorders or disabilities used in manuals such as the DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders)
The main stem or central part about which organs or plant parts such as branches are arranged
An alliance or coalition.
The centre of attention within a process (e.g. the axis of investigation)
A deer native to Asia, of species Axis axis.

ety: Coined by American political commentator David Frum in 2002 and first used publicly by President George W. Bush in the 2002 State of the Union Address. Possibly from a historical analogy to the German-Italian-Japanese axis. Extended to astrophysics by Portuguese scientist João Magueijo in 2005.

s.def: A group of states accused by George W. Bush of sponsoring terrorism and seeking weapons of mass destruction, originally defined as Iran, Iraq, and North Korea.
An anomaly in the temperature of the cosmic microwave background as the result of a preferential axis which may have shaped the development of the universe.

ety: From Middle English axel, axle, eaxle, from Old English eaxl (“shoulder, armpit”), from Proto-West Germanic *ahslu (“shoulder”), from Proto-Germanic *ahslō (“shoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs-l-eh₂, from *h₂eḱs- (“axis, axle”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian acsle (“shoulder”), Dutch oksel (“armpit”), German Achsel (“armpit”), Swedish axel (“shoulder”), Latin axilla (“armpit”), Latin axis (“axle”) (whence English axis, atelier, and via Latin āla English ala, aisle), Ancient Greek ἄξων…

s.def: Shoulder.
The pin or spindle on which a wheel revolves, or which revolves with a wheel.
ex: The mechanic replaced the broken axle on the truck.

s.def: A transverse bar or shaft connecting the opposite wheels of a car or carriage; an axletree.
An axis.
ex: the Sun’s axle

ety: From Middle English axiltre; equivalent to axle + tree. Cognate with Icelandic öxultré.

s.def: A bar or beam of wood or iron, connecting the opposite wheels of a carriage, on the ends of which the wheels revolve.
A spindle or axle of a wheel.
A stimulus or driving force.

ety: Orthographic borrowing from Classical Nahuatl āxōlōtl.

s.def: A critically endangered salamander found in the elevated lakes of Mexico, Ambystoma mexicanum.
ex: She is going on a tour to see axolotls at Mexico.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ-? Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs-der. Proto-Hellenic *aksōn Ancient Greek ἄξων (áxōn)der. English axon Derived from Ancient Greek ἄξων (áxōn, “axis”). Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- cognate with inherited English axle and other borrowed axis, aisle, ala, atelier.

s.def: A nerve fibre which is a long slender projection of a nerve cell, and which conducts nerve impulses away from the body of the cell to a synapse.

ety: From various Indian languages (e.g. Hindi आया (āyā, “dry nurse, nanny”)), from Portuguese aia (“nurse, governess”), from Latin avia (“grandmother”).

s.def: A South Asian female servant, maid or nanny, historically, often one working for Europeans in South Asia.
ex: She manufactured the Station scandal, and talked to her ayah.

s.def: A verse in the Quran.

ety: Variant spelling of Turkish Ayasuluk and Ottoman Turkish ایاصـولق (Ayasuluk), from Byzantine Greek Ἅγιος Θεολόγος (Hágios Theológos, “the Holy Theologian”), from its 6th-century basilica dedicated to St John the Theologian, supposed author of the Book of Revelation. Doublet of Agios Theologos.

s.def: Former name of Selçuk: a town in İzmir Province, Turkey, near the ruins of ancient Ephesus.

ety: Borrowed from Iranian Persian آیَتُاللّٰه (âyato-l-lâh), from Classical Persian آیَةُاللّٰه (āyatu-l-lāh), from Arabic آيَةُ ٱللَّٰهِ (ʔāyatu llāhi, “sign of God”, from آيَة (ʔāya, “sign”) + اللّٰه (allāh, “God”)).

s.def: A religious leader in Twelverism.
An authority on any subject.

ety: Derived from Kyrgyz Айдаркен (Aydarken)

s.def: A city in Kadamjay district, Batken, Kyrgyzstan.

ety: From Turkish Aydın, from Ottoman Turkish آیدین (Aydın) named for Aydin Mehmet Bey, from آیدین (aydın, “light; clarity; shining; bright; enlightened, educated, intelligent”).

s.def: Translations
A city, the capital of Aydın Province in southwestern Turkey.
A province in southwestern Turkey around the city.
A male given name from Turkish.

ety: "Appears suddenly about 1575, and is exceedingly common about 1600." Probably from use of aye (“ever, always”) as expression of agreement or affirmation, or from Middle English a ye (“oh yes”), or synthesis of both. Compare Faroese ája (“certainly, ah yes”). More at oh, yea. Online Etymology Dictionary also with these posits a possible descent from I (as if clipped from e.g. "I assent").

s.def: Yes; yea; a word expressing assent, or an affirmative answer to a question.
ex: david: […] Will he surely give him his daughter? The daughter of his house in Gilgal? soldier: Aye, surely he will.

s.def: A word used to acknowledge a command from a superior, usually preceded by a verbatim repeat-back.
An affirmative vote; one who votes in the affirmative.
ex: to call for the ayes and nays
The ayes have it.

ety: From French aye-aye, from Malagasy aiay (also ahay, haihay or hay-hay in dialect), supposedly imitative of the animal's cry. However, this is doubted by Simons and Myers (2001) who note that the animal does not emit such a sound. They suggest a derivation from Malagasy heh heh (“I don't know”), used by the Malagasy people to avoid naming the animal, which they fear.

s.def: The lemur Daubentonia madagascariensis, a solitary nocturnal quadruped found in Madagascar and remarkable for their long fingers, sharp nails, and rodent-like incisor teeth.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish aymara, possibly from Aymara or Quechua. Written attestations beginning with missionary grammars in the 1600s.

s.def: A language spoken in South America.
ex: In Potosi, Aymara is spoken in the Llica region, located north of the saltpan, and in the provinces comprising the region known as Norte de Potosi

ety: Borrowed from Arabic أَيُّوب (ʔayyūb).

s.def: Job — see also Job
Job, one of the prophets mentioned in the Qur'an
A male given name from Arabic [in turn from Hebrew], equivalent to English Job, notably borne by
A surname.
A crater on Enceladus.

ety: Borrowed from translingual Azalea, from Ancient Greek ἀζαλέος (azaléos, “dry”), because it grows in dry soil; from ἄζω (ázō, “to dry up”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs-.

s.def: A plant of the obsolete genus Azalea.

ety: [Subh-i-]Azal + -i

s.def: A follower of Azalism

ety: From French azerole, from Spanish acerola, from Andalusian Arabic الزَعْرُورَة (az-zaʕrúra), from Classical Arabic زُعْرُورَة (zuʕrūra). Doublet of acerola.

s.def: Any member of the species Crataegus azarolus of shrubs of southern Europe, related to hawthorn.
The fruit of this plant.

ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish آذربایجان (azerbaycan), from Classical Persian آذَرْبَایْجَان (āzarbāyjān), from Early New Persian آذَرْبَایْگَان (āḏarbāygān) / آذَرْبَادْگَان (āḏarbādgān), from Middle Persian [script needed] (ʾtwrpʾtkʾn) / [script needed] (ʾtwrpʾtkn /⁠āturpātakān, ādurbādagān⁠/), from [script needed] (ʾtwrpʾt' /⁠āturpāt, ādurbād⁠⁠/, “Atropates (the Persian nobleman who founded the kingdom of Atropatene)”) [whose name descends from Old Persian *Ātr̥pātah (literally “protected by…

s.def: A country in the South Caucasus in Asia and Europe. Official name: Republic of Azerbaijan. Capital: Baku.
A region in northwestern Iran, where ancient Atropatene was located, encompassing the modern provinces of Ardabil, East Azerbaijan and West Azerbaijan.
ex: Tahmâsb Coli Khân went to Azerbâïjân, and having liberated its capital, Tabriz, […]
Among these were Azerbaijan and Shirvan, where disorders had freshly broken out, […]

s.def: Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republic, the name for Azerbaijan while under the rule of the Soviet Union (1936–1991, name changed in 1990).

Hindi -ई (-ī)bor. Urdu ـی (…

s.def: A person from Azerbaijan or of Azerbaijani descent.
The language of Azerbaijan.
Of, from, or pertaining to Azerbaijan, the Azerbaijani people or the Azerbaijani language.

ety: From Azerbaijani + -ize.

s.def: to make Azerbaijani.

ety: From Old French *azimut (modern French azimut), from Arabic اَلسُّمُوت pl (as-sumūt, “the directions”).

s.def: An arc of the horizon intercepted between the meridian of the place and a vertical circle passing through the center of any object.
ex: the azimuth of a star
the azimuth or bearing of a line surveying

s.def: The quadrant of an azimuth circle.

ety: From a- + -zoic.

s.def: Destitute of any vestige of organic life, or at least of animal life.
Before the existence of animal life.
Relating to azo dyes.

ety: From Russian and Ukrainian Азо́в (Azóv), presumably from Kipchak Azaq (“lowlands”), a name applied to the region around the present town.

s.def: A town in Rostov Oblast, Russia, situated on the Don River.
A village in Ukraine (de jure)
A sea and gulf of the Black Sea, Europe; in full, the Sea of Azov.

ety: From Latin Azrahel, from Ancient Greek Ἀζαραήλ (Azaraḗl), from Biblical Hebrew עֲזַרְאֵל (ʿăzarʾēl), possibly via Aramaic (compare Classical Syriac ܥܲܙܪܵܐܹܝܠ (ʿazrāʾēl)).

s.def: The angel of death in Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, and in Islam.
ex: And his voice through all the garden is a thunder sent to bring / Black Azrael and Ariel and Ammon on the wing.

ety: From Middle English asure, from Old French azur, derived from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward, “lapis lazuli”), dropping the l as if it were equivalent to the French article l'. The Arabic is from Classical Persian لاجورد (lājward, “lapis lazuli”), from the region of Lajward in Badakhshan. Compare with Italian azzurro and Spanish azul.

s.def: The clear blue colour of the sky; also, a pigment or dye of this colour.
ex: In robes of azure.
For our blues we have the azures and ceruleans, lapis lazulis, the light and dusty, the powder blues, the deeps: royal, sapphire, navy, and marine […]

s.def: the blue sky
Sky blue; resembling the clear blue colour of the unclouded sky.
ex: When Britain first, at Heaven's command / Arose from out the azure main.

s.def: A blue colour on a coat of arms, represented in engraving by horizontal parallel lines.
ex: In Bb [Glover's Roll], the conventional letter B is used to indicate azure in most items.

s.def: The unclouded sky; the blue vault above.
ex: Not like those steps / On heaven's azure.
Not a single cloud mars the flawless azure; / Not a shadow moves o'er the moveless crops; [...]

s.def: Any of various widely distributed lycaenid butterflies of the genus Celastrina.
Any of various Australasian lycaenid butterflies of the genus Ogyris.
Lapis lazuli.
Cloudless.
In blazon, of the colour blue.
ex: ‘I forget your coat of arms.’ ‘A human foot d’or, in a field azure; the foot crushes a serpent rampant whose fangs are imbedded in the heel.’
On the fesse are two bars wavy azure for waterways.

ety: From Persian لاژورد (lâžvard, “blue color”).

s.def: A blue vitreous mineral; a basic hydrated copper carbonate, with the chemical formula Cu²⁺₃(CO₃)₂(OH)₂, used since antiquity as a blue pigment or ores to extract metallic copper.

ety: From a- + -zygous.

s.def: Odd; not one of a pair; single.
ex: the azygous muscle of the uvula

s.def: In genetics, not containing a specific allele of a gene, or only having wild type alleles (cf. heterozygous, homozygous).
Alternative form of azyme (“unleavened bread”).
